title: Top five EDGE rusher locks in gameday visit with Auburn football
description: One of the nation's top pass rushers will be on campus for one of Auburn football's most important games of the 2026 schedule.
fullText:
One of the top EDGE rushers in the nation has scheduled two visits for the upcoming fall; one of those will be to Auburn.

Auburn football has locked in a visit with 2028 five-star EDGE rusher Jalanie George for Saturday, Sept. 19, according to a report by Rivals. George will be on campus for Auburn football's SEC opener against the Florida Gators, ensuring the West Coast pass rusher will see Auburn's game-day environment at its highest level.

Auburn has been high on George's radar for several months. George put the Tigers in his top six schools in May, alongside Oklahoma, Florida, Miami, Washington, and Miami. George's interest in Auburn grew following a successful Big Cat Weekend visit this spring, and it continues to grow as Auburn is one of two teams he has locked in a fall visit with, joining Washington, who will host him on Sept. 6 for their Apple Cup game against archrival Washington State.

The EDGE rushers at Auburn have enjoyed plenty of recent success, as Keldric Faulk and Keyron Crawford were recently selected in the 2026 NFL Draft. This year's room, which includes Jared Smith and Ole Miss transfer Da'shawn Womack, is expected to be just as disruptive. The Tigers' recent success with its pass rushers is a strong pitch for George, who has the potential to be the next great EDGE rusher in Auburn's defense.

George is a five-star EDGE rusher according to Rivals and is the ninth-best player in the 2028 class. He ranks No. 2 among 2028 EDGE rushers and is the top prospect from Arizona.

Contact/Follow us @TheAuburnWire on  X (Twitter), and like our page on Facebook to follow ongoing coverage of Auburn news, notes, and opinions. You can also follow Taylor on Twitter @TaylorJones__

title: The datacenter fight could permanently transform US politics. Which party will seize advantage?
description:
The movement against datacenters are uniting Americans because they perfectly illustrate how a few individuals hold all the power to control decisions that impact our lives
Bryce Gustafson has been knocking on doors in Indiana for more than a decade. The lead organizer with Citizens Action Coalition (CAC), a consumer and environmental organization, he usually encounters a mix of reactions when he’s out canvassing; whatever issue he’s talking about, there’s always at least a few people on the other side. But at a recent festival in the rural town of Monrovia, Indiana, he was struck by an unusual spirit of unity.

fullText:
Bryce Gustafson has been knocking on doors in Indiana for more than a decade. The lead organizer with Citizens Action Coalition (CAC), a consumer and environmental organization, he usually encounters a mix of reactions when he’s out canvassing; whatever issue he’s talking about, there’s always at least a few people on the other side. But at a recent festival in the rural town of Monrovia, Indiana, he was struck by an unusual spirit of unity.

He was there about a proposed datacenter, a 550-acre (222-hectare) Google project in this small town of 1,600 people. “I had 50 people I talked to,” Gustafson told me. “Nobody wanted that datacenter in their community. And at least a half a dozen people came up to me to say, ‘Hey, I voted for Trump. What the heck’s he doing, supporting these things?’”

Gustafson said he’s had similar conversations all across the state. If there’s one thing he sees uniting Hoosiers of all stripes – from rural areas such as Morgan county to suburbs such as Franklin Township to the historically African American neighborhood of Martindale-Brightwood in Indianapolis – it’s fury over these water-guzzling, air-polluting behemoths and the tech oligarchs imposing them.

These dynamics are playing out across the US. Over the last year, intensifying waves of local opposition to big tech’s datacenter buildout have surged into a nationwide tsunami of resistance. Elites on both coasts, from leaders of the AI industry in Silicon Valley to leaders of the political establishment in Washington DC, have struggled to make sense of the backlash. First they tried to write it off as business-as-usual nimbyism: just a few local bans passed here and there, maybe some unknown city councilors losing re-election after signing datacenter deals – not such a big deal. Then senator Bernie Sanders and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez began calling for a national moratorium. Pretty soon Utah’s senate president got tossed out of office for supporting hyperscale proposals. And the movement continues to grow.

Today, three-quarters of Americans oppose local datacenter development, a swing of more than 30 points in just a year. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed datacenter bans or moratoria, while dozens of proposed projects have been killed outright. And the issue has come to define some of the highest-profile political races in the country. In the battle for US Senate in Ohio, populist Democrat Sherrod Brown has made Republican senator Jon Husted’s support of datacenters the centerpiece of his campaign, prompting warnings from the National Republican senatorial committee that “datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck”.

Other Republicans are taking notice. The Texas governor, Greg Abbott once touted the state as the “epicenter of AI development”; last week he said datacenters had “dug their own grave”. In Michigan, days after The Lever news outlet revealed that GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers held millions in AI-related investments, he announced his support for a one-year moratorium on their construction in the state.

Big tech billionaires may finally be beginning to realize that this backlash poses real complications for them. But they still don’t understand the nature of the threat they’ve called down upon themselves, because the movement against datacenters represents more than just a series of local fights against a new kind of infrastructure project. It may, in fact, constitute the best opportunity we’ve had in generations to truly shake up American politics, by redirecting the partisan anger that oligarchic forces have long used to divide regular Americans and channeling that energy instead against the billionaires that are actually the cause of so many of our shared problems.

The political science term for this strategy, coined by Jennifer McCoy and Murat Somer, is “transformative repolarization”. McCoy and Somer argue that authoritarians and oligarchs often stoke what they call “pernicious polarization” – extreme toxic polarization that uses “us versus them” rhetoric, often on social and culture war issues, to divide the public in ways that harm democracy. In the face of such intense suspicion and distrust, depolarizing a society – trying to get people to stop viewing their fellow citizens as an existential danger – may not work on its own, in the absence of a unifying struggle to address underlying grievances. Instead, McCoy and Somer argue that opponents of authoritarianism need to redraw the lines of contestation that define their politics – to shift the “us versus them” struggle from, for example, a left-to-right polarization, to a different axis of conflict that can bring a large majority of the public together against real structural threats.

When you speak to organizers and community leaders on the frontlines of local datacenter campaigns, it immediately becomes clear that they are seeing new configurations of people coming together in precisely this way. “On many issues, people come in with a baked-in partisan lens that influences their thinking,” said Ben Inskeep, program director at CAC. “On datacenters, we don’t have those firm camps formed. And so we’re seeing broad concern from Republicans, Democrats and everyone else on the political spectrum. We’re seeing folks saying, ‘Hey, I might be a Maga Republican and you might be a liberal yahoo from the big city, but if you’re coming to our community to help us fight this datacenter, you’re my best friend.’”

William Lawrence has been seeing the same thing in Michigan. The Sunrise Movement co-founder and congressional candidate made opposition to datacenters a main focus of his successful campaign for the Democratic nomination to represent the Lansing area. He’s now hammering his Republican opponent on the issue – to great apparent effect, according to a recent poll finding Lawrence leading in the district, which is now held by a Republican. “At a time when people are so polarized and isolated from each other, something that brings people together is rare,” he said. “We can all get together to watch the Spartans play at Spartan Stadium, but to get together in a context where you’re also talking about politics? That is a gift, and is not at all to be taken for granted.”

An organizer I spoke with who’s been opposing datacenter construction in Texas (who asked to remain anonymous) noted a similar dynamic playing out in his state. “I’ve never seen anything that mobilizes this many rural Texans before,” he told me. “Folks are starting to get politicized through this work. They’re realizing when they reach out to their state reps, their state senators, that these people are not batting for them. They’re batting for the tech oligarchs. And so people are realizing that the left-to-right divide isn’t as important as the divide between the working class and big corporate interests.”

The electoral implications of this process should be obvious. But for anyone too thick to draw their own conclusions, voters themselves are starting to get quite explicit. When MS Now asked a woman in Hood county, Texas, which is 80% Republican, “you’re willing to forgo every conservative issue and let the Senate fall into the hands of Democrats if that’s what it takes to kill datacenters?”, her response was immediate: “Yep. My entire community’s going to break rank.”

What remains to be seen is whether Democrats will seize this opportunity – or let Republicans regain the initiative.

“I’ve been waiting a long time for people to wake up to how they’re being ripped off,” Gustafson said. So why are datacenters the issue that’s finally waking people up?

For one, they’re essentially unique in the breadth of their odiousness, so everyone has a reason to be offended by them. Hyperscale datacenters are big industrial warehouses that can cover literally dozens of acres, generate debilitating noise pollution, and severely impact local water tables. They use obscene amounts of energy, straining local infrastructure and in many cases causing utility rates to spike. This also has devastating climate and environmental impacts, as AI developers are overwhelmingly meeting their energy needs with dirty fossil fuel generators that spew outrageous amounts of planet-warming emissions and severely impact local air quality.

Then there are the process concerns: use of eminent domain, the provision of taxpayer subsidies, and big tech’s near-ubiquitous practice of pushing local officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) that shroud deals in suspicious opacity.

And all of this is for what? Though the development of datacenters creates temporary construction work, once developed, the facilities do not provide communities with significant long-term jobs. The only thing these sites produce (other than many shades of pollution) is added compute for a technology that we’ve all been told will soon put billions of people out of work. In the meantime, as we wait to see whether that dystopian future materializes or it was all an economy-wrecking bubble, AI is largely being experienced as the thing making the internet more annoying, our jobs more stressful, surveillance more terrifying, and big tech billionaires – already widely despised – more powerful than ever. It’s not hard to understand why this doesn’t constitute a very compelling case for datacenters.

What it does provide is a perfect canvas on which to illustrate the broader problems with our political and economic system: how a few individuals have all the money and power to control the decisions that impact our lives. “Datacenters are the physical manifestation of the greed and the hubris and the power of the AI oligarchs,” Gustafson said. “That gets people thinking about why we are allowing these tech billionaires to just run roughshod over our state.”

What emerges from this process is a budding sense of solidarity that can extend far beyond the localized concerns that might have brought someone into a particular fight. Gustafson described how organizers from Evansville, a city in south-west Indiana, began supporting groups across the border in Kentucky when fights started ratcheting up there. Elsewhere, a farmer who became the leader of a datacenter fight in Henry county, Indiana, attended a meeting about a proposed project in a neighboring town. “Next thing you know, she’s helping that community, showing up for them, because it’s so much easier getting through this when you have somebody who’s been there and understands,” he said.

As Inskeep put it: “When one campaign ends, people are saying, ‘Hey, we fought ours, now that it’s done, we’re going to go to the next county and help them.’” And that starts a snowball effect. “People are seeing that they’re stronger together. It’s a beautiful thing.”

Clearly, these fights have created an opening for the left. But the politics around datacenters are still very much up for grabs. Democrats should have a strong inherent edge, given that – on this issue, like so many others – Donald Trump has forcefully aligned himself with his buddies in the billionaire class. The president’s aggressive plans to accelerate big tech’s datacenter buildout include opening up federal lands for hyperscaler construction, axing public participation processes in permitting, and even waiving Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act requirements on the radically absurd grounds that datacenter approvals need to be expedited for national security reasons.

But other conservative forces have been ahead of the curve. Steve Bannon has long been working to put Maga’s populist wing out front in opposing both datacenters and AI more broadly. The Texas organizer I spoke with told me he sees a significant number of people coming into datacenter fights casting blame not on big tech oligarchs, but on China or the United Arab Emirates, in ways that can feel decidedly xenophobic or Islamophobic. “This is an opportunity, but it’s a short-lived opportunity and we need to seize it,” said Inskeep. “Because this can also be used against us. If we are not effective at doing the political education and helping folks through that process, I do think you could have a far-right, nationalist, anti-immigrant person use this issue to come to power and then implement horrifying policies.”

Needless to say, for Democrats to seize this opportunity, they first must actually take a unified stance against datacenters. And unfortunately, many Democratic leaders remain just as in-bed with big tech billionaires as their GOP counterparts. Maine’s Democratic governor, Janet Mills vetoed the datacenter moratorium passed by her state legislature. Michigan’s Democratic governor, Gretchen Whitmer was accused of dismissing her constituents’ concerns about the many datacenter projects she has supported. The Democratic minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries opposes a datacenter moratorium and appointed the aggressively corporatist Josh Gottheimer and big tech-backed Zoe Lofgren to help develop House Democrats’ AI platform.

And there are some races where Democrats are squarely on the losing side of the issue. In Wisconsin, the Democratic nominee for governor, David Crowley, is already being blasted in ads by his Republican opponent for having said he wants Wisconsin to “become an AI and a data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe”. Crowley won his gubernatorial primary after the entire Democratic establishment united to oppose the left-leaning candidate in the race, Francesca Hong, on the grounds that old “woke” posts – including a call to “cancel Thanksgiving” – made her unelectable. But Crowley’s troubles demonstrate why Democrats need to update their assumptions regarding what kinds of past statements make for real electoral liabilities. After all, nobody is actually going to cancel Thanksgiving. But making Wisconsin into a hub of hated datacenters? That feels like a very real possibility to a lot of Wisconsin’s swing voters.

When I asked Lawrence what he would want to say to party leadership on this point, his response was simple. “I would say, listen to the people. Nobody wants companies from Silicon Valley coming in, bullying us, making decisions that are going to impact the next century of our communities. Just listen to the people. You’ll be popular.”

So will Democrats take the chance they’ve been given? For the first time in generations, the billionaire class has overreached in a way that Americans of all stripes and ideologies are finding equally repulsive. They’ve created a perfect opening to repolarize the public – not just against Trump, but against the oligarchic and authoritarian systems that produced him in the first place.

The opportunity before us is singular. What a monstrous mistake it would be not to seize it.

Aaron Regunberg is a former Rhode Island state representative and a contributing editor at the New Republic. He is the director of Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project, but is writing here in his personal capacity

title: ProCook outdoor pizza oven review: a budget-friendly model that brings the pizzeria home
description:
This no-frills pizza oven gets the basics right and is more than good enough for most people
• The best pizza ovens – tested 
• Ooni Koda 2 review
The market for pizza ovens tends to be dominated by a handful of specialist brands, so it can feel like a gamble to buy from a lesser-known manufacturer or a retailer that offers a wider range of goods.

fullText:
This no-frills pizza oven gets the basics right and is more than good enough for most people

The best pizza ovens – tested 

 Ooni Koda 2 review

The market for pizza ovens tends to be dominated by a handful of specialist brands, so it can feel like a gamble to buy from a lesser-known manufacturer or a retailer that offers a wider range of goods.

The ProCook outdoor pizza oven is no gamble, though. It’s every inch a capable, compact and versatile pizza oven, despite being just one product in an offering that includes pretty much everything from storage jars to squeegees.

This outdoor pizza oven conforms to ProCook’s usual direct-from-manufacturer pricing. Coming in at a comparatively reasonable RRP of £249, the oven punches far above its weight in terms of functionality. As well as foldable legs for storage, it has room for 12in pizzas and a manual rotating stone for more even cooking. Turn the stone as the pizza bakes for an evenly blistered crust or simply adjust it as needed. At 12kg, it’s also light enough to take to a friend’s house or on a camping trip.

I tested the ProCook in the same way I test other pizza ovens for the Filter. As well as assessing the quality of the cook by making pizzas with different toppings – cheese and tomato at about 430C; a slow-cooked veggie pizza at 350C with onion, pepper and tomato to caramelise and soften the topping; and a salami pizza at about 400C – I rated the oven for ease of assembly, overall use, lighting, temperature control and storage. I also recorded heat-up times, although, as it was tested in cooler months, these may be longer than in the warmer months.

The ProCook outdoor pizza oven is cheaper than similarly sized models, but you’ll need to invest in an infrared (IR) thermometer for the best results. In tests, the oven heated from cold to 430C in about 25 minutes, which is about average for a compact gas-powered oven, and the rotating stone that sits on its own turntable doesn’t have much impact on heat-up times either way.

The rotating stone has no raised edges, which means that you’ll need to be fairly accurate when launching pizza. Any other dishes you cook in the oven, such as chicken or fish, will also need to fit on the round stone.

ProCook doesn’t offer much in the way of accessories. There’s no cover, but there is a great-value pizza peel for just £10.

Dimensions: 43.2 x 65.5 x 31.2cm (WDH) / mouth 35 x 10cm (WH)
Maximum capacity: stone diameter 32cm (working capacity, 12in pizza)
Features: manual rotating stone, control dial ignition

 Fuel: gas

 Spare parts: control knob, rotating knob and fixing nut 

 Weight: 12kg

For what is effectively a budget-friendly model, the ProCook outdoor pizza oven gets all the basics right. It lit first time via the built-in ignition, but can also easily be lit with a match should this fail. I especially liked that there was no need for a turning peel – a utensil that helps you turn the pizza in the oven – and that the rotating stone is powered by hand, making the whole thing pleasingly low-tech, with no need for batteries or recharging.

Some of the pizzas I made burned at the corners, but this is because the bought dough I tested with (for consistency) was shaped into rectangles, rather than circles. Overall, pizzas cooked well, although with less rise than I’ve achieved in pricier ovens. This was most noticeable on the cheese and tomato pizza. I also found thicker toppings needed a lower temperature and longer cook, with some of the vegetables remaining firm while others began to char. The salami-topped pizza was the best of all, with evenly melted cheese and just a slight singe on one edge.

The dial for the rotating stone sits at the side of the pizza oven, relegating the control for the gas to the rear. This means you can’t see the flame as you light the oven and adjust the heat. You may need two people – one on the gas control, and one watching the oven’s flame size as it’s altered.

Another drawback is the size of the oven’s mouth. It’s relatively narrow and short, with the space becoming even tighter around the stone. This makes launching and retrieving pizza trickier than with rival models such as my overall favourite, the Gozney Arc Lite, and the Ooni Koda 2. On the plus side, if you later invest in a bigger oven, the ProCook will at least mean you’ve honed some serious pizza-launching skills.

The ProCook outdoor pizza oven comes with a two-year guarantee, with spare parts also available via customer services once it’s out of warranty. Sadly, the rotating stone cannot be replaced if it becomes damaged or breaks. Despite being an outdoor oven, ProCook’s instructions advise storing it indoors, out of harsh weather conditions, such as heavy rain, strong winds and direct sunshine.

The ProCook is my favourite budget pizza oven. The combination of good design and low price makes it a smart buy for beginners – and those who’d rather spend big on toppings for their next pizza party. It might not deliver the wow results of more expensive ovens, nor come with lots of fancy features, but unless you plan to cook pizza regularly, it’s unlikely you’ll miss them.

Another point to bear in mind is that this is very much just a pizza oven. Unlike those models that double up as versatile outdoor ovens, this ProCook model offers limited space on the stone for roasting pans, slow cooking in ambient heat, and sizzling side dishes – so if you want to experiment with a wider range of dishes, this probably isn’t the oven for you.

However, if pizza is what you want most of the time – and who doesn’t? – the ProCook outdoor pizza oven is an excellent choice for families, busy households and anyone keen to master homemade pizza.

Her home has hosted hundreds of appliances while her garden has seen a succession of pizza ovens, barbecues and heaters put through their paces. It takes a lot to impress her – many appliances have tried and failed

title: Dozens evacuated from Grand Canyon National Park after flash floods
description: No injuries were reported but park officials warned people against accessing the closed areas.
fullText:
Dozens of people were evacuated Saturday from Grand Canyon National Park after parts of the canyon were struck by flash flooding.

Bright Angel Canyon was hit by flash floods Saturday afternoon, according to the National Parks Service (NPS), but no injuries were reported. The NPS said it was conducting an aerial evacuation of "approximately 50 individuals" in the Phantom Ranch area.

In a social media post, the NPS said "the entirety of the North Kaibab Trail and Phantom Ranch are closed until further notice."

The Phantom Ranch is a historic and extremely popular lodge close to the bottom of the Grand Canyon by Bright Angel Creek.

Park officials asked people to stay away from the closed areas and said the operator of the lodge, which is usually fully booked months in advance, will inform guests about the state of their reservations.

Grand Canyon National Parked ranked fourth-most visited national park in the United States with 4,430,653 recreational visits in 2025.

title: Hong Kong's independent bookstores, a refuge for Chinese readers, are under threat
description: Chinese university student Fleming Cheng found the political books he had only glimpsed online in a Hong Kong bookstore last year.  Before visiting Greenfield Book Store, Cheng had only managed to see...
fullText:
HONG KONG (AP) — Chinese university student Fleming Cheng found the political books he had only glimpsed online in a Hong Kong bookstore last year.

Before visiting Greenfield Book Store, Cheng had only managed to see the books' covers online after bypassing Beijing's internet censorship using a VPN. At the store, he picked up a title offering a critical account of China. He stood there devouring dozens of pages from another, about a pro-reform Chinese leader who fell from power for sympathizing with the protesters during the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement in 1989.

Cheng said he saw perspectives diverging from the mainland's official narrative.

Hong Kong's independent bookstores, many of them tucked away from busy streets inside buildings, have long offered a refuge and a window to a freer world for some mainland Chinese readers seeking ideas suppressed at home.

But these spaces now are under threat following a wave of bookseller arrests over alleged sedition under a 2024 national security law. Critics say their plight reflected the city's broader crackdown on dissent that began after Beijing imposed a separate 2020 security law. Authorities say the two laws are vital to stability.

Greenfield was one of four bookstores targeted by police in just four months. Although bail was granted, the 50-year-old shop in July announced it would close at the end of its lease. Another bookstore, Have A Nice Stay, set up by former journalists, had announced plans to shut down Sunday, citing "elusive red lines" and financial challenges, even before its booksellers were arrested on the same day as Greenfield's.

"If the Hong Kong government desperately tries to bring every aspect of the city into close alignment with the mainland, or even to the point where the two become indistinguishable, that would be a tremendous loss for us mainlanders too," Cheng said.

Hong Kong, a former British colony that returned to China in 1997, was once known for its freedoms of publication and expression.

But in 2015, bookseller Lam Wing-kee and four others affiliated with Causeway Bay Books disappeared. The store was known for selling politically sensitive titles. Lam later told reporters he was held by Chinese authorities, providing explosive details that contradicted official Chinese accounts. Gossipy books about Chinese politics soon dwindled on Hong Kong's shelves.

After the 2020 security law, leading activists were arrested and civil society groups disbanded. Titles about the Tiananmen crackdown and works by pro-democracy politicians were pulled from public libraries. At the city's annual book fair, some smaller book businesses were barred from exhibiting, and a pro-Beijing newspaper labeled an independent book fair a form of "soft resistance."

Despite the pressure and increased official inspections, many pressed on, with some continuing to organize activities alongside selling books.

But the arrests hit Book Punch in March, Hunter Bookstore in June, and Greenfield and Have A Nice Stay in July. The authorities accused the booksellers of selling seditious publications, according to government statements and media reports.

Authorities say statements with "seditious intention" to incite hatred against or the overthrow of the governments of China and Hong Kong are prohibited. But they have not specified the books they consider as "seditious," leaving observers to find clues in news reports quoting anonymous sources.

Secretary for Security Chris Tang said the law is clear about what constitutes seditious intent and reiterated there would be no banned book list. He said booksellers should ensure the titles they sell do not harm national security, just as those selling food need to ensure the food won't cause a stomach ache or be poisonous.

A bookseller, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of government retribution, said they struggled to judge what was seditious. Still, they became more cautious about whether to sell certain books on China's modern politics. Their landlord was also reviewing whether to continue to rent the space to them after being harassed.

In an emailed reply, the government condemned any "smearing" and false remarks regarding the work in safeguarding national security. It said the security laws clearly stipulate that human rights, freedoms of speech and publication should be protected.

The offenses linked to seditious intention expressly protect expression of opinions or even criticism against government policies, it said.

University student Iris Wang from neighboring Guangdong sensed tighter control over Hong Kong. To her, Hunter encouraged people to think, instead of just selling books like its mainland peers. She bought a postcard about being courageous and a manga there.

Some mainland readers also visit the stores for non-political reasons, such as for their niche books or simply for their calmness.

Hong Konger Brian Leung found companionship in independent bookstores, saying each had its own character. When arrests happened at the shops he visited, he said he felt something he cherished and that Hong Kong deserved was being rejected.

"Part of what I have grown used to in Hong Kong is lost again," he said, adding that the bookshops have not "incited" him because readers can judge for themselves.

In Taiwan, widely seen as the freest publishing hub for Chinese-language books, some publishers have filled the gap as restrictions deepened in Hong Kong after the 2020 security law took effect. Some readers fear one day Taiwan cannot send books to Hong Kong as freely as before.

Taiwan's publishers released six times as many books about Hong Kong between 2020 and 2024 as in the previous five years, according to Cheng Tsu-Bang, a sociology professor at Tunghai University in Taiwan.

"The publication of books seems to have become a very important medium of communication between Taiwan and Hong Kong, or a medium of mutual support," he said.

In July, Taiwan's broadcaster FTV reported that a logistics firm stopped taking orders to ship books from Taiwan to Hong Kong bookstores under investigation. It also demanded a full book list before delivering to other Hong Kong premises, the report added.

One Hong Kong author who moved to Taiwan and has published books there is Lee, who spoke on condition of not using their full name out of fear of government retribution.

Lee has written about Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement, saying the independent bookstores served as a bridge to bring works about Hong Kong to the city and connect diaspora writers to their home.

The writer compared the collapse of civil society to a boulder rolling downhill, crushing things in its path. Lee said bookstores were a small flower field where people could breathe and try to safeguard what remained.

"It's now like being told very directly and cruelly that perhaps this borrowed time is coming to an end," Lee said.

title: Venezuela's interim president says US energy deal will last 25 years
description: Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez said on Saturday that an energy agreement with the U.S. would remain in force for 25 years, target an increase in crude output
fullText:
CARACAS, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez said on Saturday that an energy agreement with the U.S. would remain in force for 25 years, target an increase in crude output ‌to 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) and preserve the country's sovereignty over its natural resources.

Rodriguez hailed the ‌accord in a late-night address as a "historic" deal that would help revive the economy and boost government revenue, saying it would help shape ​the country's future.

"This 25-year bilateral project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with a production target of more than 1.5 million barrels per day," Rodriguez said on state broadcaster VTV.

"That figure relates solely to the bilateral agreement between Venezuela and the United States."

Rodriguez added that the agreement's target of 1.5 million bpd was only an initial goal and that ‌the broader plan also included the ⁠development of eight greenfield oil blocks as part of a wider expansion of the country's energy sector.

President Donald Trump on Friday announced plans for the U.S. to take partial control ⁠of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, betting that American companies can help revive the South American nation's battered energy industry while providing a new source of crude to help lower U.S. fuel prices.

Trump provided few details on the agreement, saying only that ​the U.S. ​had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels ​of Venezuela's proven oil reserves through a partnership ‌with private business.

Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves, but it produces only about 1.25 million bpd - far below its potential - after years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions.

Rodriguez said the agreement could generate about $209 billion in revenue for the Venezuelan state, based on a benchmark oil price of $65 per barrel, though she acknowledged crude prices could fluctuate. She said roughly $19 from each barrel produced and sold under the arrangement would flow directly to Venezuela, providing ‌a significant boost to government revenue.

She said that the country retained "ownership ​of and sovereignty" over its natural resources, "while leveraging capital, technology and ​operational expertise to support the recovery of a ​strategic industry that has been severely affected by sanctions."

Earlier on Saturday, dozens of pro-government groups ‌gathered in downtown Caracas to protest against the ​U.S. presence in Venezuela.

Rodriguez welcomed ​the agreement following Trump's announcement, saying it would bolster economic growth and increase government revenue.

title: 12 jobs that are set to shrink over the next decade
description: New job projections show which may experience employment declines from 2025 to 2035, whether due to automation or another reason.
fullText:
The Bureau of Labor Statistics published new job projections for 2025 to 2035.

Employment of word processors and typists is expected to fall the quickest.

Automation is a key reason some of the jobs are expected to decline.

Automation is set to reduce the need for some jobs over the next decade, like order clerks and switchboard operators.

New Bureau of Labor Statistics projections show which jobs may rapidly grow between 2025 and 2035, and which may shrink. Word processors and typists are projected to experience the largest percent decline, falling 34%. It's one of 206 jobs that the Bureau of Labor Statistics classified as having "very high" exposure to AI.

The 12 jobs with the largest projected percent declines typically aren't high-paying. Most of them earned less than the national median annual wage of $50,980 in 2025.

Employment of foundry mold and coremakers, as well as metal and plastic patternmakers, is projected to decline, partly due to businesses' ability to leverage 3D printers. For word processors and typists, BLS said other workers are taking on these duties, and "traditional typing methods continue to be replaced by automated processes through use of machine learning (ML) technologies."

Telemarketers and mining roof bolters are set to see changes in demand for different reasons. For telemarketers, BLS said the "share decreases as the Do Not Call registry from the FCC continues to grow, and companies increasingly use alternative digital marketing methods." For roof bolters, it's due to a preference for surface mining over underground work.

Overall, US employment is projected to rise 3.5% over the decade, down from 10.9% growth in the decade earlier. Some jobs are expected to increase due to the care of an aging population.

The private healthcare and social assistance sector is expected to have a bounty of opportunities, accounting for 37% of the 5.9 million jobs projected to be added to the US.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Opinion - What happens when Republican senators have nothing left to lose? Not much.
description: Often called the “Wounded Bear” or YOLO (“you only live once”) Caucus, these lawmakers have nothing to lose. But despite a greater willingness to voice objections to Trump nominations and policies, th...
fullText:
For years, we have been told that Republican senators privately object to many of President Trump's policies and appointments but do not resist because Republican voters would punish them at the ballot box. There are at least four senators who have little to fear from elections or Trump right now, yet remarkably little has changed.

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) is retiring in January. Sens. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas) both lost primaries to Trump-backed opponents and will not run again. And Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) opted against seeking reelection after Trump threatened to support a primary challenger against him.

Often called the "Wounded Bear" or YOLO ("you only live once") caucus, these lawmakers have nothing to lose. But despite a greater willingness to voice objections to Trump nominations and policies, they almost never vote "no" when it counts.

Trump's recent nomination of Todd Blanche to be attorney general illustrates the pattern.

Cornyn and Tillis demanded a written commitment ending Trump's proposed $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund as the price for their support. Neither focused much on the provisions granting Trump and his family immunity from IRS investigations. Widely denounced as a slush fund to reward Trump allies and supporters — including potentially rioters who attacked Capitol police on Jan. 6, 2021 — it was labeled by Cornyn as "politically tone-deaf" and a "payout pot for punks." Tillis called it "stupid on stilts;" McConnell declared it "utterly stupid, morally wrong." Cassidy accused Blanche of showing "poor judgment" in helping negotiate it, questioned his independence, and expressed concern about the Justice Department's "bringing suits against political enemies."

Every Democrat, along with Republicans Susan Collins (Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), opposed Blanche. One more "no" vote would have killed the nomination. Hospitalized and unable to vote, McConnell did not take a public position. Cornyn and Tillis voted yes, after Blanche ordered the Justice Department to rescind the fund — an order that can easily be reversed, as Trump has suggested he might do.

With the nomination hanging in the balance, Cassidy put it over the top, holding back tears as he explained that an acting attorney general might be even worse than Blanche.

All four appear no more willing to sink a Cabinet-level nomination, block a major Trump initiative, or defend the Senate's institutional role now than they were before.

McConnell voted against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., as well as Trump's Canadian tariff and global tariff "emergencies." As he surely expected, none of his votes changed the outcome.

Cornyn almost never opposed Trump before losing his primary. After losing, Cornyn blocked two controversial ambassadorial nominees for the Foreign Relations Committee, but let them advance after getting "assurances" on AIDS funding.

A member of the Judiciary Committee, Tillis blocked the nomination of Ed Martin to serve as the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia in 2025 because of his comments about the January 6 attack on the Capitol. After deciding not to run again, Tillis delayed (but did not stop) the nomination of Kevin Warsh as Federal Reserve chair, until the Justice Department dropped its criminal investigation of then-Chair Jerome Powell.

Before losing his primary, Cassidy, a physician and chair of the congressional committee overseeing public health, helped block the nomination of Casey Means for surgeon general. But after expressing grave doubts about RFK Jr.'s views on vaccines, he still cast the decisive vote to confirm him as Secretary of Health and Human Services.

After losing his primary, Cassidy declined to schedule hearings on Heidi Overton's nomination to head the Food and Drug Administration, calling her support for Trump's executive order on vaccines "almost disqualifying." Cassidy also joined Democrats in trying to block Bill Pulte's nomination for acting Director of National Intelligence, an effort that failed in a 49-49 tie.

But Cassidy folded on Blanche's nomination. And after initially supporting a war powers resolution to block further military action in Iran, Cassidy backed down after receiving a briefing he had demanded in a heated confrontation with Trump.

In short, whether it involves Trump's willingness to wage war without congressional approval, appoint his former criminal defense attorney to head an already politicized Justice Department, withhold or redirect funds appropriated by Congress, or demand confirmation of dozens of nominees en bloc, the wounded bears have largely acquiesced.

And why not add Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) to the list? The dean of the Senate, Grassley has championed government oversight of waste, misconduct and abuse by whistleblowers and inspectors general who, he claims, should be "almost wholly free of supervision." Nonetheless, when Trump removed 18 inspectors general in January 2025, Grassley sent only a letter of concern, which was not even answered for eight months. He did not employ his signature tactic, holding up nominees for other offices, to ensure the watchdogs would be protected. When his current term ends in 2028, Grassley will be 94. We wonder what accounts for his muted response.

In a closely divided Senate, the YOLOs have enormous leverage, but they are not using it to challenge executive branch overreach. No doubt party loyalty, relationships with Republican colleagues, and a reluctance to help Democrats still matter to them. But it should be deeply troubling that compliance seems to have become Republicans' default setting.

If senators with nothing to lose won't insist on preserving the Constitution's checks, balances and separation of powers, who will?

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

title: Opinion - Electric vehicles are flaming out —let’s ‘Make Internal Combustion Engines Great Again’
description: If you are a builder, promoter or buyer of electric vehicles, good for you. Science and technology do march on. But occasionally, at what cost? While it’s quite easy to understand the rationale for bu...
fullText:
If you are a builder, promoter or buyer of electric vehicles, good for you. Science and technology do march on. But occasionally, at what cost?

While it's quite easy to understand the rationale for building EVs — perceived innovation, business plans, and profit — it's still natural to question the promotion and purchasing of said vehicles. At least for some.

Much of the EV market is still wrapped around "virtue signaling" as it relates to the ever-moving target of "climate change." The entitled, lecturing left in Hollywood certainly buys into that narrative, as almost every movie we see these days features an EV or hybrid driven by one of the main characters. "See," they signal. "We are all about protecting the environment."

A serious question for Hollywood and the EV huggers is this: what if a percentage of those vehicles are ultimately worse for the environment? Or more costly, more dangerous on the highway, or a fire hazard?

The latter concern was recently the subject in a piece for The Washington Post, titled: "They were told to park outside. Then their cars burst into flames." But it was the laugh-out-loud sub-headline that betrayed the lengths some will seemingly go to in order to protect the carefully cultivated myth about electric vehicles. "Modern vehicles don't need to be moving — or even turned on — to catch fire. That's fueling lots of safety recalls and tough choices."

The piece goes on to stress that the danger of these "modern vehicles" —no specific mention of "EVs," just "electronics" — bursting into flames while not running has grown so high that "park outside" warnings have increased into the millions. That's right, millions.

Leaving aside the "burst into flames" issue associated are a number of other negatives that many on the left prefer we not address. Let's start with the battery that powers these "modern vehicles." When being disposed of, these batteries are considered "toxic" and a "hazardous waste."

The weight of one of these flammable batteries starts at 600 pounds, with the high end topping out around 3,000 pounds. Just the battery. Just like the tens of thousands of "green" wind turbines desecrating the American landscape while killing thousands of birds, the deeper you dive into the details, the more alarming the reality becomes.

Of course, the greatest irony of the "green" energy revolution, be it windmills, solar panels or electric vehicles, is that much of it has to vampire off fossil fuels to be created and, ultimately, to survive. Another fact some on the left would prefer remains unsaid.

But going back to the "modern vehicle" issue, we should never forget that it sure seemed that the "environmentalists" in the Biden administration were seeking to sabotage — or outright destroy — the gasoline-powered car market by forcing a 56 percent reduction in new vehicle emissions by 2032, with the goal of having 60 percent of all new vehicles to electric by 2030. What could possibly go wrong by taking all internal combustion-powered vehicles offline?

It turns out that upwards of 75 percent of EV battery components are made in — you guessed it — China. Pardon the pun, but forcing the U.S. population into EVs will only put the leadership of China more firmly in the driver's seat of world domination.

Moving beyond the fire hazard of these EV batteries, their toxicity, the damage their tremendous weight does to tires and roads, and their unreliability in very cold and very hot weather, we come to a serious issue of national and personal security issue: the Biden administration's attempt to install "kill switches" into all "modern vehicles" as a way to prevent drunk driving.

In January, Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky posted on X: "Federal law says new cars after 2026 must monitor drivers and shut down if the car disapproves. Your dashboard should not be judge, jury, and executioner."

Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis then amplified this position with his own post on X: "The idea that the federal government would require auto manufacturers to equip cars with a 'kill switch' that can be controlled by the government is something you'd  expect in Orwell's 1984, and yet…"

The obvious question in the minds of DeSantis, Massie and millions of other Americans: Who is in charge of this "kill switch?" What if the "nanny state" targets certain individuals, groups or political parties? If you don't believe this possible, simply cast your mind back to the draconian dictates that came out of the COVID-19 panic.

All of which begs the most important question of all: What was wrong with our "old fashioned" vehicles? Our gasoline-powered cars and the internal combustion engine? Absolutely nothing.

Is there a place for electric vehicles? Of course. They are a wave of the future, but they should not come to represent the whole ocean. We need to hedge our "modern vehicle" bets.

With each passing day, internal combustion powered vehicles continue to prove themselves attractive, valuable and needed. They are generally less expensive than EVs, less likely to spontaneously burst into flames, more reliable in blackouts and weather extremes, and more protective of civil liberties. Not to mention the basic need to transport oneself from Point A to Point B.

While some loudly sing the praises of the "modern vehicle." I say, "Make Internal Combustion Engines Great Again." Old may not only be new again — it might literally help to preserve our liberties while protecting our lives.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

title: Your guide to Reading Festival 2026
description: The festival runs from Thursday 27 August to Sunday 30 August at Richfield Avenue.
fullText:
One of the UK's biggest festivals returns to Berkshire this week.

Reading Festival will welcome about 100,000 people, with headliners Charli XCX, Chase & Status, Raye, Florence and the Machine, Fontaines D.C. and Dave taking to the stage.

The annual festival will run from 27 August to 30 August at Richfield Avenue.

Here is some information to help you prepare for the event.

Weekend and Early Entry ticket holders can enter the campsites from 18:00 BST on Wednesday.

Weekend ticket holders can enter campsites from 08:00 on Thursday.

The campsite is open 24-hours-a-day and individuals can arrive at any time after they are permitted to enter.

The campsite will close at midday on Monday.

Those who are leaving and returning after 20:00 on Sunday will need to get their hands stamped on their way out to be able to return later.

Those with day tickets cannot re-enter the arena once they leave.

However those with a weekend ticket can leave and re-enter the arena and campsites.

Reading Festival is a fully cashless event.

Festivalgoers can pay by debit or credit card and can also use Apple or Google pay.

The festival is operating a Challenge 25 policy, and IDs must be in date.

The following forms of identification are accepted:

Full driving licence or provisional licence

A proof of age card bearing a PASS hologram

A Ministry of Defence identity card

A national identity card issued by an EU member state

Disposable BBQs are not permitted on site due to the hot weather and dry ground conditions.

Campfires are also not permitted and anyone found lighting one will be evicted.

Organisers are urging festivalgoers to be mindful of cigarette disposal and to not dispose of cigarette butts on the ground.

Prohibited items for the arena and campsites include:

Animals (other than registered hearing dogs or guide dogs)

Drones and other flying devices

Fitted gas canisters/cylinders are only permitted in camper vans in the campsites

Fireworks/pyrotechnics, flares/distress flares, smoke bombs

Gas cylinders/canisters of any size for non-cooking purposes (including nitrous oxide)

Glass bottles, jars, containers over 100ml. Items under this measurement, such as small perfume bottles, nail varnish, and small mirrors will be permitted

Illegal substances (drugs) and legal highs, herbal highs, new psychoactive substances and unidentifiable substances.

You cannot bring alcohol for personal consumption into the arena only.

Empty reusable plastic and metal bottles are allowed into the campsite and arenas.

All customers are permitted to bring a small amount of food for personal consumption into the arena.

Accessibility customers are permitted to bring additional food in excess of the usual amount into the arena.

All customers are permitted to bring a sealed, unopened 500ml bottle of water or soft drink into the arena.

Drug detection dogs will be operating throughout the event.

The full list of what you can and cannot bring can be found here.

Reading Borough Council has asked people travelling to the town centre ahead of the festival to be prepared for longer travel times.

Parking restrictions, including no stopping for pick-ups, will be in place around the Richfield Avenue site as normal.

The Hills Meadow Car Park will be the dedicated area for drop offs and pick ups and people attending the festival can either walk to the site or use free shuttle buses.

Other festival car parking will be available at Kings Meadow and Mapledurham and a pedestrian bridge has been built to ensure easy and safe access at the latter.

Reading Buses are running a shuttle bus service which picks up and drops-off at:

Service 97/98 – Thames Side Promenade, Reading

Service 98 – Reading Station North, stop ND

Service 97 – Sainsburys Friar Street, Reading

At Kings Meadow, an official festival boat service will be provided free of charge for people going to the site.

The Thames Path will be closed between Scours Lane and the far end of Thameside Promenade from 19:00 to 06:00 on Thursday to Monday.

The council and festival organisers have produced official travel information, along with a wider information page.

The BBC's coverage of Reading and Leeds festivals is available on BBC iPlayer and on BBC Sounds.

Charli XCX and Raye to headline Reading and Leeds Festival 2026

Festival granted music extension despite noise concerns

title: Trump says 'Meet the Press' host Kristen Welker will be reported to FCC
description: President Donald Trump sharply criticized Kristen Welker, the moderator of NBC's "Meet the Press," after abruptly exiting an interview with her earlier this year.
fullText:
President Donald Trump said "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker will be reported to the Federal Communications Commission over her coverage of his endorsements ahead of the midterm elections.

"Kristen Welker, the Unpopular 'Hostess' of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has 'mixed results' on his Endorsements of Candidates, when the recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Aug. 30.

USA TODAY has reached out to NBC for comment.

Trump added, "Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment. Unfortunately, she is not the only one."

Despite Trump's post, the FCC doesn't have much legal power to take action against Welker as an individual, but his comments escalate his criticism of the journalist.

In early June, Trump made headlines when he abruptly exited an "MTP" interview with Welker after a tense back-and-forth, when the NBC anchor pushed back on the president's comments about California election security.

The FCC is an independent agency that oversees broadcast, radio and other networks. Disney and ABC sued the agency over what they called an unconstitutional "retaliatory campaign" against the network in an Aug. 18 lawsuit.

Critics say the FCC has become increasingly political during Trump's second term under the leadership of Brendan Carr, who Trump referenced in the Truth Social post as he wrote that "The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation."

Trump does have a strong 2026 endorsement record, but some candidates he supported lost recent primaries.

In Wyoming, Megan Degenfelder, who leads the state's department of public instruction, lost in a Wyoming Republican primary for governor. Rep. Cory Mills lost his reelection bid in Florida as did Tennessee congressman Andy Ogles, a controversial House member. In Minnesota, longtime Trump ally and MyPillow founder Mike Lindell also lost a GOP primary for governor.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Trump says 'Meet the Press' host Kristen Welker will be reported to FCC

title: Republicans fret as Talarico bombards airwaves and Paxton awaits Trump team’s cash
description: Democrat James Talarico has dominated the airwaves in the race with Ken Paxton for the open Senate seat that could decide which party controls that chamber.
fullText:
Senate GOP leaders gave President Donald Trump a clear warning before the Texas primary election in May as he weighed endorsing Ken Paxton over longtime incumbent John Cornyn: If the state attorney general won, Trump's political operation would have to bankroll the expensive general election campaign to help make the controversial Paxton more appealing to voters, according to multiple Republican sources.

But more than three months later, MAGA Inc.'s wallet has so far been closed. And Republicans are growing anxious — as the Democrat, state representative James Talarico, has had the airwaves largely to himself for weeks, spending roughly seven times more than the GOP since June.

"They keep saying they'll spend, but they haven't," said one senior GOP source involved in the discussions.

With polls now showing the race that could help determine which party controls the Senate to be tight, Trump is beginning to put more of his attention in Texas, headlining a Thursday fundraiser in Houston that he described as an effort to help Paxton. And a separate, pro-Paxton outside group unveiled a new $800,000-ad blitz on Friday, the latest example in recent days of Paxton getting more air support.

"I'm going to help Ken Paxton and I'm going to spend a lot of time in Texas," Trump told reporters at the White House before leaving for Houston.

The fundraiser was not for Paxton's campaign, but for the Republican National Committee. A recent Supreme Court ruling gave groups such as the RNC new power to coordinate with campaigns on spending, a development that Republicans hope will be especially beneficial to candidates like Paxton who are financially behind in must-win races.

Yet it's still unclear how much Trump's outside group, MAGA Inc., will spend of its $400-million-plus war chest to come to Paxton's defense. The state attorney general has faced a long list of scandals over the years, including a 2023 impeachment vote by the Texas House of Representatives over allegations of bribery and corruption. The state Senate later acquitted him of all the charges.

The lack of spending has frustrated top Republicans, who had insisted repeatedly to the White House that a Cornyn victory would be far less expensive to a party looking to deny Democrats the four seats they need to flip the chamber.

MAGA Inc. has declined to publicly preview any spending plans for the midterms. But it has begun ramping up its activities, starting with an event scheduled for Monday in Michigan with Vice President JD Vance as the headliner. A spokesman for the group, Alex Pfeiffer, said in a statement that MAGA Inc. "will be hosting events throughout the nation" ahead of the midterms.

But MAGA Inc.'s decision to wait to spend its vast resources has effectively given Democrats and Talarico a chance to dominate the Texas airwaves since other big-spending GOP outside groups have also sat out for now.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and the super PAC tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, the Senate Leadership Fund, both of which strongly backed Cornyn in the primary, have been looking for MAGA Inc. to take the lead in the general election. A spokesperson for the Senate Leadership Fund said it was "confident" Paxton would win but otherwise declined to comment on any spending plans.

Since the June start of the general election season, Texas voters have been seeing mostly Talarico spots across the airwaves, with Democrats outspending Republicans on advertising by about $31.5 million to $4.7 million in the race, according to AdImpact data.

Talarico's campaign, fueled by its robust fundraising, accounts for the majority of the spending, about $31.3 million. With the airwaves virtually uncontested, his campaign has run ads thousands of times introducing the first-time statewide candidate to voters while emphasizing cost of living concerns.  On Saturday, Talarico unveiled his first negative ad about Paxton, attacking him over the allegations of corruption.

Paxton's campaign, bruised and drained from the runoff, has spent just over $150,000 on advertising since June, a far cry from the staggering sums spent by his rival.

Paxton has taken to conservative media to plea for help.

"We're a little behind on TV," Paxton told Newsmax earlier this month.

While Talarico continues to dominate the airwaves, outside spending for Paxton has picked up in recent days. As of last week, at least four different groups had entered the fray to target Talarico on TV, including the main pro-Paxton super PAC, Lone Star Liberty PAC, and Truth and Courage PAC, a super PAC aligned with Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX).

All of the initial attack ads target Talarico over his opposition to a 2025 bill to ban Texas land sales to certain people from China and other countries deemed a national security threat. The bill passed the state House, and Gov. Greg Abbott signed it into law months later.

The ads nonetheless portray Talarico as enabling an active foreign encroachment on state land.

"Communist China is buying up Texas because Talarico sold us out," a narrator says in an ad from Truth and Courage PAC.

Talarico's campaign has countered that Paxton is the one who is too close to China, citing a 2019 trip he took there with other state attorneys general that concerned some of his own staff, according to Fox News. "There's a reason Republicans call him 'Commie Ken,'" Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement.

Republicans are also eyeing America PAC, the super PAC funded by Elon Musk, as a potential aid to Paxton. While a spokesperson declined to comment on the group's plans, it has increasingly attacked Talarico's record on social media in recent days, including in a post that vowed: "Texans will reject this."

Meanwhile, the main super PAC supporting Talarico, Lone Star Rising PAC, unveiled it first general election ads Tuesday, including one that calls Paxton "the most corrupt politician in Texas." The ads are part of an initial seven-figure buy running statewide on streaming and digital platforms.

Republican strategists in Texas, granted anonymity to frankly discuss the race, have said for weeks that Paxton needs more advertising from their side countering the moderate image that Talarico is projecting on TV.

One longtime Republican operative in the state said a major issue for Paxton is lack of support among "non-MAGA Republicans" who probably won't vote for Talarico but could sit out the race. Polls have shown Paxton is not consolidating support from his party as much as Talarico is.

The operative said it was "frustrating to watch" because many Texas Republicans have known since the start of the election cycle that Paxton would be a weaker nominee than Cornyn if he won the primary.

Another Texas Republican strategist, who is working on down-ballot races, predicted Talarico's polling position would soften once the onslaught of attack ads takes a toll. Right now, Talarico is "gaining the positives without the negatives," especially in the eyes of independents and moderate Republicans, the strategist said.

"It has to become a drumbeat that voters can't ignore," the strategist said of the anti-Talarico ad blitz. "The volume and the frequency matter."

Sen. Tim Scott, the chair of the NRSC, didn't say directly when asked if his committee would help bankroll Paxton in an air war during the final weeks of the campaign.

"The strategy in Texas is strong," Scott told CNN. "It's going to be very well-funded. We have no actual reasons to be concerned about Texas. Paxton is working hard."

Asked if Trump's organization should begin to spend money in the state, Scott said he anticipated the money would begin to flow.

"We know that they're going to be fully engaged," the South Carolina Republican said.

But as party leaders await Trump's help in the race, whether more traditional Republicans will come to Paxton's aid also remains to be seen.

Asked by CNN earlier this month if he planned to campaign on behalf of Paxton, Cornyn deadpanned.

Correction: This story has been corrected to note that polls show no clear leader in the race between Talarico and Paxton.

title: Mica Miller’s siblings allege pastor husband forced final hospitalization before her 2024 death
description: Mica Miller's siblings allege JP Miller had her involuntarily committed as part of a coercive control pattern during their troubled marriage.
fullText:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Mica Miller's siblings are speaking out about the late worship leader's troubled marriage, alleging her estranged husband, South Carolina pastor John-Paul "JP" Miller, had her involuntarily admitted to a mental health center.

Mica's family discusses the alleged hospitalization in "Death of the Pastor's Wife," a three-part true-crime series that premiered Wednesday on Netflix. The documentary delves into her life, marriage and April 2024 death, which authorities ruled a suicide.

Mica's family describes the hospitalization as part of a broader alleged pattern of coercive control during her marriage.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Her final hospitalization was involuntary, the siblings allege. They claim Miller contacted a mental health center and initiated the admission against his wife's wishes.

According to her siblings, Mica was diagnosed with bipolar disorder while she was engaged to Miller, who reportedly took an active role in overseeing her care. They claim she was hospitalized multiple times during the relationship, including shortly before the couple married in 2017.

In a handwritten affidavit accompanying her divorce filing reviewed by Fox News Digital, Mica alleged that she had been abused "emotionally, sexually, spiritually, financially, and physically."

The family further said that while Mica was hospitalized, Miller took possession of her vehicle, phone and laptop. Her siblings said the computer contained intimate photographs of her. Mica later reported the alleged incident to police, according to the Netflix series.

Miller reportedly declined to participate in the documentary. Fox News Digital has reached out to his attorneys for comment.

The documentary relies on interviews with Mica's relatives, friends, former Solid Rock Church members and divorce attorney, the streaming platform said.

Mica, 30, was found dead at Lumber River State Park in North Carolina April 27, 2024, two days after serving Miller with divorce papers.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

The Robeson County Sheriff's Office concluded that she died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound and closed its investigation. Miller has denied involvement in her death and has not been charged in her death.

He is, however, facing an unrelated federal prosecution over his alleged conduct toward Mica before her death.

A federal grand jury indicted Miller in December 2025 on charges of cyberstalking and making false statements to investigators, according to a release from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of South Carolina on Dec. 18, 2025.

Prosecutors allege he posted a nude photograph of Mica online without her consent, had tracking devices placed on her vehicle, contacted her more than 50 times in one day, interfered with her finances and damaged her tires.

Miller's alleged cyberstalking put his wife in "reasonable fear of death and serious bodily injury," according to the federal indictment, which added that his conduct "would be reasonably expected to cause [Mica Miller] substantial emotional distress."

Federal authorities say that Miller also lied to investigators when he was questioned about damaging Mica's tires. Investigators later found that Miller purchased a tire-deflation device online and sent messages to others referencing her vehicle, according to the indictment.

If convicted, Miller could face a maximum sentence of five years in prison on the cyberstalking charge and two years for making false statements, along with fines of up to $250,000. Miller pleaded not guilty and remains free on $100,000 bond.

Mica Miller 911 Call Reveals Final Moments Before Her Death As Nc Authorities Challenge 'Conspiracy Theories'

Mica's relatives are also supporting proposed South Carolina legislation, Bill 702, known as "Mica's Law."

The legislation would recognize coercive control, including sustained psychological, emotional and financial manipulation, within the state's domestic violence laws. The bill was referred to the state Senate Judiciary Committee but did not advance during the 2026 legislative session.

title: Wrexham boss Parkinson 'probably under pressure' for first time
description: With no wins yet this season, ex-Wales striker Iwan Roberts believes Phil Parkinson is probably under pressure for the first time as Wrexham boss.
fullText:
Phil Parkinson is probably under pressure as Wrexham manager for the first time, according to former Wales striker Iwan Roberts.

Friday night's 2-1 home defeat by Birmingham left Wrexham winless and without a clean sheet in four matches across all competitions in 2026-27.

Roberts told BBC Radio Wales: "I think he [Parkinson] is probably under pressure for the first time since he's been at Wrexham.

"He's had some incredible success at the football club. I think he's quite stubborn in his way, in his tactics, he doesn't like to change, and I don't mind that because they have been so successful.

"But I've said it too many times, when you're chasing a game, you're behind with 15, 20 minutes to go, he still persists with the back three, instead of maybe trying something different, going to a back four and getting another body further forward."

Do Wrexham have a defensive problem?

Latest Wrexham news, analysis and fan views

Parkinson himself bemoaned his side's defensive failings that contributed to Phil Neumann's brace for the Blues as "two of the softest goals" conceded in his reign.

Roberts believes such failings are not new, saying: "The Achilles heel last season, and the reason they didn't get into the play-offs, is they had the sixth worst defensive record in that league and this is the scary statistic - at home, only bottom club Sheffield Wednesday conceded more goals than Wrexham."

Roberts also believes Parkinson's squad is already too large with the manager still in the hunt for new players.

"Wrexham were the highest spenders last summer and I think there's only four clubs that have spent more this summer, and he's still on about bringing more players in," said Roberts.

"A squad of 33 players, I think that's too much. I think that in itself can cause you problems."

fullText:
Hamburg are in advanced talks to buy Arsenal midfielder Fabio Vieira in a 10m euro (£8.6m) deal.

The Gunners are actively trying to offload the 26-year-old before Tuesday's transfer deadline.

It is understood there is a growing expectation at Emirates Stadium that a deal with the German side will be agreed.

Vieira spent last season on loan at Hamburg, making 29 Bundesliga appearances for the club, scoring seven goals.

The Portuguese midfielder joined Arsenal from Porto in 2022 for £34m but failed to establish himself at the Emirates.

He made 47 appearances for the Gunners – but only five of those were Premier League starts.

Vieira was loaned back to Porto during the 2024-25 campaign before his spell at Hamburg last season.

title: Marquez wins third straight Aragon Grand Prix
description: MotoGP world champion Marc Marquez boosts his title hopes by winning at the Aragon Grand Prix for the third year in a row.
fullText:
MotoGP world champion Marc Marquez boosted his title hopes as he won at the Aragon Grand Prix for the third year running.

The victory helped Ducati's Marquez close the gap between him and championship leader Jorge Martin to 19 points from.

The 33-year-old's eighth triumph at MotorLand came after an intense battle with Aprilia's polesitter Marco Bezzecch.

Marquez, who won Saturday's sprint, nearly made contact as he impressively overtook Bezzecchi at high speed on lap six.

He moves up to 237 points, leapfrogging Bezzecchi (232) to climb to second behind Aprilia's Martin (256), who finished fifth.

"I heard his bike on turn 15 so I tried to cross the line, but when we were close, the slipstream was pushing each other very much and it was strange," Bezzecchi said.

"Marc, with the experience that he has and the speed that he has, today he was unbeatable."

Bezzecchi, 27, finished the race in third behind Marquez and KTM's Pedro Acosta.

title: Tearful Federer inducted into Hall of Fame
description: Roger Federer says being inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame is "one of the greatest honours" of his life.
fullText:
Roger Federer has been inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame, describing the moment as "one of the greatest honours" of his life.

The 20-time Grand Slam singles champion, who retired in 2022, was tearful at the ceremony in Newport, Rhode Island, as he reflected on his glittering career in front of tennis greats including Billie Jean King and John McEnroe.

After making his main tour debut in 1998 at the age of 16, Federer won a record eight men's Wimbledon singles titles, plus six Australian Open crowns, five US Opens and one French Open.

"This is one of the greatest honours of my life," Federer, 45, said.

"They call this the Hall of Fame, but fame was never the goal. My goal was to spend my life doing something I love, with people who love it as much as I do."

Only Spain's Rafael Nadal, with 22 majors, and Serbia's Novak Djokovic, with 24, have won more men's Grand Slam singles titles than Federer.

He won his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon in 2003 and spent 310 weeks as the world number one - a record until it was surpassed by Djokovic.

Federer also won Olympic doubles gold for Switzerland with Stan Wawrinka at Beijing 2008 and singles silver at London 2012.

He was part of the Swiss team that won the Davis Cup for the first time in 2014.

Federer, who started out as a 13-year-old ball boy at an ATP tournament in Basel, reflected on the lesser-known statistics from his career during his speech.

"I'm talking about the numbers that really paint a picture. Between 1998 and when I first went on the ATP Tour, and when I retired in 2022, I wore more than 5,000 headbands," said Federer.

"That's more than [Bjorn] Borg and [John] McEnroe combined.

"And if you think that's impressive, I wore probably over 7,000 pairs of socks. That's probably twice as many as most of my opponents, because I doubled them up.

"But really, there's no way to measure what it means to be here. It's hard to put it into words."

Federer wiped away tears as he thanked his wife Mirka, tennis idol Stefan Edberg and "every ball kid who ever stood through" his matches.

Federer also said he was "incredibly lucky" to have played with different generations of tennis players, from Andre Agassi and Lleyton Hewitt to Andy Roddick, Nadal and Djokovic.

"I need tissues and sunglasses and everything to protect me right now. This is such a mess," Federer joked.

"As you can tell, I'm still writing my love letter to tennis. My time as a player is done, but tennis will always stand at the intersection of everything I care most about: my family, our friendships, the past 40 years, the future we're building.

"Tennis for me is responsible for it all."

title: Coventry sign Mfuni on loan from Man City
description: Coventry City sign English defender Stephen Mfuni on a season-long loan deal from Manchester City.
fullText:
Coventry City have signed English defender Stephen Mfuni on a season-long loan deal from Manchester City.

The 18-year-old has appeared once for his parent club, making his senior debut as a substitute in last season's 10-1 win against Exeter City in the FA Cup.

The England Under-19 international was then loaned to Watford, where he played eight times in the Championship.

Mfuni becomes Coventry head coach Frank Lampard's 11th signing since they were promoted to the Premier League at the end of last season.

"I feel blessed to be here, it's exciting. These are moments you dream of and to do it with such a good team and a good squad, I'm looking forward to it," said Mfuni.

"I spoke to the gaffer, he wants me to show what I normally do on the pitch, whether I'm at left-back or centre-back, and for me to keep being me and do what I do."

Coventry are 18th in the Premier League after losing their opening two games of the season against Arsenal and Hull City.

Their next game is away at City on 5 September.
