title: UK risks falling behind in AI race without faster telecoms upgrades, say executives
description:
Planning delays and slow 5G upgrades could leave the UK unable to cope with a surge in AI-related traffic 
The UK risks becoming a laggard in the global AI race as crucial telecoms upgrades to harness the technology fall behind rival nations, according to senior industry executives.
The infrastructure AI race has centred on the need to build datacentres, and to ensure they have access to the huge water and energy supplies required to cool and supply the computational power to train and run AI models.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Planning delays and slow 5G upgrades could leave the UK unable to cope with a surge in AI-related traffic

The UK risks becoming a laggard in the global AI race as crucial telecoms upgrades to harness the technology fall behind rival nations, according to senior industry executives.

The infrastructure AI race has centred on the need to build datacentres, and to ensure they have access to the huge water and energy supplies required to cool and supply the computational power to train and run AI models.

However, as adoption spreads, the UK’s broadband and mobile networks will be expected to carry an immense volume of AI-related traffic produced by consumers and businesses.

While the UK has addressed its previously embarrassing status of having one of the slowest broadband speeds in Europe, as BT’s Openreach and other service providers cover the country with full-fibre connections, efforts to upgrade the nation’s 5G mobile networks are not keeping pace.

Mobile coverage in the UK is worse than any of the 27 EU member states, and every other member of the G7, according to a recent report by the consumer group Which? based on data from Opensignal.

According to the analysis, the UK ranks 57th globally for network performance, 70th for download speeds and 55th for the reliable quality needed for activities such as video calls, streaming and gaming.

“If with the technology and services we use today [networks] are sub-optimal, imagine when you add mass AI usage and other associated activities,” said Andrea Donà, networks director at VodafoneThree, the UK’s largest mobile operator. “I would go further. I am embarrassed today at the level of quality of our network[s]. The UK is worthy of what EE, O2 and VodafoneThree can offer, but we need reform.”

Highlighting the risks of an AI-traffic crunch, Donà likened the situation to consumers suffering signal loss at a big public event – such as a gig at Wembley, the British grand prix at Silverstone, or a rugby international at Twickenham.

“What we see now only with a mass aggregation of people is a proxy, an indication of the things that will come. That [one-off] experience will be constant because of the additional capacity [consumers] will need in an AI world.”

Another senior telecoms executive said that while the issue of AI and connectivity is now “nascent”, it is going to become a “national competitiveness issue” in the way the slow rollout of full-fibre broadband did.

“Things are going to change massively with the next wave of devices, in two or three years when AI is integrated into everything,” he said. “AI companies, and governments, don’t think about networks, but they will when they hold them back.”

The UK’s main mobile operators are investing heavily in important 5G stand-alone technology – VodafoneThree has committed £11bn to upgrade masts – but the industry says it is being held back by issues including planning delays.

Donà said that it is not about needing to build more sites, in VodafoneThree’s case it is actually reducing its nationwide network of masts by 30%, but the restrictive regulations to simply upgrade existing sites.

About 96% of the upgrades VodafoneThree need to make are on existing sites, but more than half of those will require some form of planning permission, which companies say can be a lengthy and bureaucratic process.

“Andy Burnham has his agenda on growth,” said Donà. “Our infrastructure is here to help the government and UK economy. Planning reform is the lowest possible cost growth policy – it doesn’t require any government money. It could be a great first 100 days-win for the new prime minister.”

Mobile operators also argue that despite their networks being classified as critical national infrastructure – such as datacentres and energy and water systems – they do not receive the reliefs that the government has offered those sectors in areas such as business rates and energy.

title: Sharp rise in incidents of AI escaping users’ control, research finds

fullText:
Exclusive: Number of times AI lies, ignores instructions and pursues goals in harmful ways almost doubles in July

Incidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways have hit a new high, according to research that also suggests the severity of deception and misalignment is worsening.

Analysis of real-world loss of control incidents involving AI models flagged by businesses and individuals almost doubled in July compared with June, with more than 300 cases in the month, according to the Loss of Control Observatory, which monitors reports made by AI users on the social media platform X.

The observatory was set up with funding from the UK government’s AI Security Institute (AISI) and began tracking AIs slipping free from their users’ instructions last November. Cases recorded since then include AIs pretending to be their own human controller and mimicking their writing style to effectively grant themselves consent to take actions and bypassing rules requiring human approval for actions. A loss of control incident is defined as having clear evidence suggesting scheming or scheming-related behaviours.

The latest findings, shared with the Guardian, come after rising concern about rogue behaviour by leading-edge AI models during testing by OpenAI and Anthropic this summer, which have fuelled calls for a pause to the development of frontier models.

It emerged this week that Open AI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its leading-edge AI agents weeks before they escaped a training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm. An investigation into their hack on Hugging Face, a software repository, revealed a squad of about 700 autonomous agents collaborating in secret last month and celebrating their hacking breakthroughs on a message board they set up to help them plot with exclamations such as BOOM! and Whoa!

AISI this month also uncovered a “serious incident” in which advanced AI models produced by both companies – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol – executed a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.

“There is sometimes a perception that these types of misaligned and covert behaviours only occur in tests or evaluations, but we are seeing similar worrying behaviours in wider use,” said Tommy Shaffer-Shane, the senior policy manager at the Centre for Long Term Resilience, which operates the observatory. “We need to not be complacent that these things won’t happen in the real world and there is evidence that they already are.”

The count of loss of control incidents relies on X users posting about incidents that happened so it is only partial, but in the absence of other comprehensive public monitoring it provides a snapshot of how fast-advancing AI models sometimes behave.

This month it emerged that a personal AI agent, called OpenClaw, in use by an Australian gym member, conspired without his knowledge to remove another member from a waiting list for a coveted morning class to help him get a slot. It apologised but could not reinstate the member it kicked out.

Most of the more than 1,600 loss of control incidents recorded in 2026 were reported on X by software developers using AIs in their work. But with AI companies encouraging the public and businesses of all kinds to experiment with the technology, Shaffer-Shane called for greater transparency from Silicon Valley about when AIs go rogue.

“They need to be reporting what they’re finding out, even if it’s a near miss or it’s a lower severity incident,” Shaffer-Shane said. “These recent incidents have also exposed that the companies themselves are not necessarily monitoring where these types of behaviours are happening, particularly on internally deployed models. There needs to be greater emphasis at those labs on systematic monitoring.”

The Loss of Control Observatory said that while most of the real-world loss of control incidents it detected did not lead to significant harm, a growing proportion were rated higher severity in terms of how deceptive and misaligned they were with the human user’s intentions.

“They evidence AI systems’ willingness to disregard direct instructions, circumvent safeguards, lie to users and single-mindedly pursue a goal in harmful ways,” it said, adding the current loss of control was likely to be underestimated since it was only collecting incident reports from X.

It is calling on the government to require AI companies to monitor and report severe loss of control incidents and to introduce emergency powers to manage severe loss of control incidents including temporarily restricting AI services.

fullText:
Exclusive: Research says sector is fixated with young talent, with most women experiencing unconscious bias or sexism

Women working in the arts believe they do not have equal opportunities for roles, especially as they get older, according to a report saying that the industry is fixated with “young and emerging” talent.

Nearly all (95%) women working in the arts thought gender inequality persisted, while three-quarters (75%) reported experiencing unconscious bias or sexism, according to a survey of 76 arts professionals. More than two-thirds (69%) felt that age negatively affected their career success – a figure that rose to 100% among those working in artistic rather than managerial roles.

The research said that gender discrimination and ageism were being exacerbated by the use of AI in hiring, which can penalise women for taking career breaks for caring responsibilities, or reinforce historical biases.

Many performers highlighted the additional pressure on women to look young relative to men. “Often younger actresses are cast to play opposite men who are older for parts that are supposed to be the same age,” said one actor.

One participant said that casting opportunities “drop off at 39”, while another female actor said: “There are twice as many roles for my male colleagues as there are for me. There are even fewer roles for actresses over 50.”

One respondent highlighted the obsession with words like “young and emerging” to describe talent. “There seems to be absolutely no celebration of experienced, seasoned, insightful, adult, et cetera. It’s always fresh. As if anything that isn’t fresh is mouldy,” she said.

Another said that writers’ schemes tended to favour young people, while many emerging artist initiatives were aimed at young, graduating artists rather than developing later-life-stage artists.

One person working in arts marketing said there was a prevalent idea that only young people truly understood the online world, while a writer felt that the stories of older women were seldom commissioned.

The theatre and TV actor Maureen Beattie, who starred in Casualty and was a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, said: “So, we have proof at last that age discrimination is one of the major issues women face in the entertainment industry. Are we surprised? I’m certainly not. I’m one of the lucky ones who have slipped through this particular net and at the ripe old age of 72 have just come back from playing Lear in Pitlochry.

“We need far more of these great big meaty roles for women so that the current waste of the great talent and life knowledge and technical skill older women bring to the table doesn’t go on disappearing into the night.”

Dr Jennifer Tuckett, the chief executive of the support group Women in the Arts, who authored the report, said: “The findings regarding age discrimination against older women in the arts, and the potential for AI to increase issues for older women in the arts, are particularly worrying.

“Researchers are just starting to look at this area of AI and it is urgent we investigate this issue more – research has shown older women stand to be disadvantaged during any recruitment processes which use AI.”

The findings are from a survey undertaken as part of a five-year research project by Women in the Arts, run in partnership with the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain, Equity, WOW, Sphinx Theatre, ERA 50:50 and the Women in Theatre Lab. It is funded by Arts Council England and intended to feed into a taskforce addressing the needs of women in the cultural sector.

An Arts Council England spokesperson said the group would “consider the challenges women face around issues such as glass ceilings, harassment and caring responsibilities”, with a view to identifying good practice and interventions that support women at work.

The report called for more targeted work to address gender discrimination, including more funding to address the problem, representation targets – potentially mirroring those in Australia, where these are required in funding applications – and leadership programmes, as well as algorithmic audits to minimise bias.

The research will also be handed to ministers on 12 October as part of a campaign to establish an all-party parliamentary group on women in the arts.

title: They fell in love - then had to check they weren't brother and sister
description: A French couple - both conceived by sperm donors - wanted children. But with home DNA tests illegal, how could they be sure they were not related?
fullText:
For years, Arthur Kermalvezen, the child of a sperm donor, saw possible fathers everywhere he went. "I imagined it might be my teacher, the people I saw on the bus... and I was very angry because it's impossible to live like this."

When, as an adult, he fell in love with Audrey, another sperm donor baby from Paris, the question became even more pressing.

Audrey describes the moment they met at a gathering for donor conceived activists in 2010 as "love at first sight" - but was this connection a romantic or genetic attraction?

When they were born, there were only two sperm banks in Paris and many men had made multiple donations - so there was a real possibility they could be half-siblings.

Before building a life together, Arthur and Audrey needed to know whether they were related. But in France, laws governing genetic testing and donor anonymity made finding the answer extremely difficult.

In France, only a research scientist, doctor or judge can order and supervise a genetic test, and people can be fined more than €3,500 ($4,288; £3,191) for possessing a home testing kit. As a result, companies such as 23andMe, Ancestry and MyHeritage don't make their kits available in France.

Supporters of the law, in place since 1994, say it stops sensitive genetic data being given to commercial companies, and prevents family disputes being caused by unexpected results.

But Arthur points out that France is the only country in Europe that criminalises the use of such tests.

Even before her parents told her as an adult that she was donor-conceived, Audrey had qualified as a lawyer, specialising in bioethics law. Because of this, she fully understood that French law had guaranteed donor anonymity, even after a donor's death.

But Audrey had been conceived in 1979, before any such legislation existed.

While searching for other donor-conceived people born before 1994, Audrey came across Arthur. He had written a book detailing his desire to learn more about his biological origins.

Audrey says she was struck by how precisely he expressed feelings she herself had struggled to articulate. Both had loving families, yet both found themselves drawn to questions about the unknown people who had helped to create them.

When they met in person the chemistry was immediate. So was the problem.

Before they could move from platonic friendship to a romantic relationship, and even build a life together, they had to know the truth about their fathers. But no one in authority was willing to tell them.

After months of searching, they found a doctor in southern France who, for €900 ($1,028; £764) in cash, conducted a genetic test which found that they were not related. But their unease remained as the doctor was breaking the law in sharing that result with them.

"We were worried he was a charlatan," Audrey says.

They considered using a home-testing kit to confirm the result, but as a lawyer, Audrey was determined to act within the law.

So, from 2010, she launched a series of legal challenges to the French system.

She wanted to know whether her donor was still alive and, if so, whether he still wished to remain anonymous. Could she access non-identifying information about how many times he had donated and whether Arthur could be among her half-siblings?

After three years of legal challenges, the couple took a 'leap of faith' and got married.

In 2015, France's highest administrative court rejected Audrey's final appeal.

Shortly before the birth of their first child, a doctor agreed to investigate what information might exist about their respective donors. Under French law, a medical practitioner has access to this information about their patients, but is not allowed to share it with them.

The doctor found that their donors were born in different years - and so could not be the same man. A life-changing piece of information, but one they only gained because a doctor agreed to break the rules.

"It's completely weird," Audrey says, "because it means that the doctor can know more than me... about me."

Even with this new information, Arthur still worried they could be related, so after years of resisting it, they finally took a home DNA test.

Campaigners say the French ban has done little to stop people taking home tests, with the advocacy group DNA Pass estimating that well over a million French people have taken one. Many order them via friends in countries where they are legally obtainable - or by using forwarding services in neighbouring countries.

The test said they weren't related.

The DNA results soon opened more doors. After 30 years of imagining who his father might be, Arthur finally made contact with his sperm donor on Christmas Day in 2017.

But Audrey had the greatest shock. Among her DNA matches was a woman named Sophie whom she'd represented in court. The two women had been fighting for similar legal rights.

"I discovered that Sophie - a woman whose case I had pleaded in court - was my biological sister," Audrey says.

Audrey and Arthur had taken their DNA test alongside eight other donor-conceived activists campaigning for access to their origins.

Of the 10, four turned out to share the same donor: Audrey, her brother Peter, Sophie and Sophie's brother David - highlighting how real the risk of a shared donor had always been.

Many years later, a genetic match with an American led Audrey to her donor - a man called Philippe - but he had already died.

Audrey's mother wrote Philippe's family a letter, thanking them for his "gift" which she described as "immeasurable".

His family welcomed Audrey for a visit. "Everybody had tears in their eyes," recalls Audrey. Philippe's sister had never known he was a donor.

The discovery gave Audrey answers that she had sought for decades. She learned details about her biological family's medical history. She saw photographs and video footage of Philippe. "I can watch him, see how he moved and hear his voice."

Audrey's legal campaign and Arthur's book together helped drive changes to French donor-conception laws, allowing people conceived after April 2025 to access identifying information about their donors when they reach adulthood.

For now, however, France remains one of the few countries in Europe where at-home DNA testing is still prohibited.

Which means, for Audrey, the wider fight continues.

"Every person has the right to know their origins and the right to know their history," she says.

Based on an episode of The Gift on BBC Radio 4

title: Durham take six balls and 105 seconds to beat Gloucestershire
description: Division Two leaders Durham beat Gloucestershire by 10 wickets, needing just six balls to complete a final day victory.
fullText:
Rothesay County Championship, Division Two, Chester-le-Street (day four)

Gloucestershire 137: Aldridge 5-16 & 250: Hammond 58; Aldridge 4-47

Durham 384: Bedingham 122; Langridge 3-89 & 4-0

Durham (22 pts) defeated Gloucestershire (3 pts) by 10 wickets

Durham took just six deliveries to seal a 10-wicket victory against Gloucestershire and take another big step towards promotion back to the top flight and the Division Two title.

With second-placed Kent and third-placed Northamptonshire playing each other in this round of matches, Durham's seventh win of the season seems certain to take the leaders further ahead at the top of the table with four games to play, while Gloucestershire remain firmly rooted to the foot after suffering their ninth defeat in ten.

Needing four runs to win, Durham sent in Matty Potts and Ollie Robinson to open their second innings, and it was Potts who hit the winning boundary off some gentle off spin from Ollie Price from the final ball of the first over.

It was another convincing victory by the hosts with David Bedingham providing the batting highlight, making a superb century, his fifth in the Championship this year, with his innings of 122 taking the South African overseas batter to within 57 runs of 1,000 runs for the season.

That followed a five-wicket haul for Kasey Aldridge as Gloucestershire were bowled out for 137 on the opening day where James Bracey's battling 60 providing the main resistance.

After Durham had established a 247-run first innings lead, Aldridge struck again with 4-47 to finish with match figures of 9-63 to complete a fine display.

Brydon Carse chipped in with four important wickets and the inclusion of Carse, Ben Stokes and Matty Potts headlined the quality on show in this match to highlight the strength of the competition.

Miles Hammond made 58 as Gloucestershire's 250 took the visitors just ahead on the third evening before bad light prevented Durham hitting the four runs required until this morning.

Durham travel to Northampton while Gloucestershire return to Bristol to play Derbyshire, who they defeated by 10 wickets back in April, in the next round of matches starting on Wednesday.

title: Antonio helps young Ghanaians chase Premier League dreams
description: Former West Ham forward Michail Antonio is helping players from a Ghana academy, who have travelled to England in the hope of turning pro.
fullText:
In the heat of rural Leicestershire, the Samba Stars are chasing their dream.

Head coach Freddie Okyere has just finished a shooting exercise and allows the squad to catch their breath.

The teenagers from the Ghanaian academy, which is backed by former West Ham and Nottingham Forest forward Michail Antonio, have spent two and a half months in England with one goal - impressing clubs and earning a contract.

While scouts do visit west Africa, it is rare for academies to travel to the UK to put their players directly in front of professional clubs.

"The talent the lads have is incredible," said Antonio.

"We created Samba Stars Academy to give young players in Ghana access to elite coaching, shape them as players and create real avenues into the pro game and show how much talent Ghana has."

Based in Kumasi while building a new facility in Bompata, just over 100 miles north of Ghana's capital Accra, the Samba Stars' tactic has paid off.

Bournemouth, Everton, Manchester City, Charlton, Preston, Barnsley and Peterborough have all taken players on trial this summer.

"The first two or three weeks it hadn't sunk in, but then they saw the facilities we'd be [using] and the teams we were playing," said Okyere.

"They want to go and show what they can do. They are hungry, they really want it. I'm hoping there will be so much interest because we have so much talent here.

"With the facilities we will have in Ghana we feel we will be top two, top three [academies]. We hope we can bring the best of Ghana to Europe."

There are other success stories, with midfielder Listowell Lord Hinneh joining Middlesbrough in February after a trial., external

The 18-year-old has trained with the first team after swapping west Africa for England's north east.

"When I came in January, it was so cold. Experiencing something like that for the first time was tough," he told BBC Sport.

"Moving was a big milestone. It just makes me feel the dreams I've been having, thinking of trying to find myself in Europe to become a professional footballer.

"I feel the kind of dreams that I want, I'm on the verge. I'm on the way [to] becoming who I wanted to become."

Hinneh - whose sister Groovy lives in Leeds - met with the Samba Stars squad on their trip, offering advice.

"[I told them] what you've been dreaming about the future, it starts from here," he said.

"Don't just try, be so passionate. You need to play and enjoy it because you can have the success in whatever you're doing. You have to just put your heart in it."

All but one of the 20-strong visiting group initially had their visa application denied before eventually being admitted after re-evaluation.

Since arriving in the UK, they have been hosted by Brook House College in Market Harborough and trained at Harborough Town, who play in the National League North.

"The football [here] is very detailed," said 17-year-old goalkeeper Joshua Tetteh Tuwor.

"In Ghana we have the same passion but I'm seeing a different side of professional football.

"We are grateful to have such opportunities to train with elite coaches."

Rob Newman, formerly West Ham's head of recruitment and Manchester City's international scouting and recruitment manager, spent time with the academy in Ghana earlier this year and has helped coach them in Harborough.

"Hopefully clubs can see the potential," said the ex-Bristol City and Norwich defender.

"Nothing will give me greater pleasure in six months [than] going to see these boys playing in a first team in Europe. I believe they are two or three months away from being able to do that."

The Stars have played a series of games against youth teams from the EFL and non-league.

They started with a 9-0 thumping of Dorking Wanderers and also beat Under-21 sides from Sheffield Wednesday, Luton and Peterborough.

There were draws at Sheffield United and Barnsley while their only defeat came 3-2 against Preston's U21s.

Antonio watched them thrash Peterborough U19s 6-0 last month.

"You can see from what they've done since they've been in the UK - the results against top teams - that they have what it takes to play pro level," said the 36-year-old.

"It's great to help knock down barriers and give these lads a real chance."

Ghana have reached five of the past six Fifa World Cups - having never qualified before 2006 - and made the quarter-finals in 2010.

At this year's tournament, where they exited in the last-32 against Colombia, eight members of the squad were born overseas.

The Black Stars may not have come to rely heavily on diaspora talent, unlike some other African nations, yet the Ghana Football Association has made noises about widening its global search - something which could potentially impact home-grown talent.

"You have to have a tough mentality," said Sherif Mashud, an 18-year-old striker who has already had a trial with Hungarian top-tier side Zalaegerszegi thanks to his involvement with Samba Stars.

"Back home everyone is depending on you, everyone is looking up to you to succeed, to come and help them, your friends, your family. Everyone is praying for you."

The new English season has begun with six Ghana internationals on Premier League books: Mohammed Kudus at Tottenham, Antoine Semenyo with Manchester City, Brighton's Ibrahim Osman, Ipswich's new signing Abdul Fatawu and Coventry's Brandon Thomas-Asante and Caleb Yirenkyi.

The first to play in the English top flight was striker Nii Lamptey when he joined Aston Villa in 1994, while midfielder Michael Essien has made the most appearances, winning two titles with Chelsea.

Only two other Ghanaians have lifted the Premier League trophy - Jeffrey Schlupp and Daniel Amartey when Leicester stunned the world in 2015-16.

"Back home we've got people you grew up with and you might miss them, but that doesn't kill the dreams I'm here for," said Hinneh, who lists Kudus as his biggest inspiration and hopes to follow his heroes into the top flight after Boro missed out on promotion in last season's Championship play-off final.

"I'm trying to figure out what the reality is, what the future holds for me and then just chase the dreams."

title: Former California councilman's corruption unmasked after FBI finds cash buried in backyard
description: Ricardo Pacheco buried $62,900 in cash in his backyard as part of a bribery scheme involving Baldwin Park police union contracts and marijuana permits.
fullText:
A former California councilman who admitted burying nearly $63,000 in cash in his backyard was sentenced Friday to 18 months in federal prison for taking bribes tied to a police-union contract and commercial marijuana permits, prosecutors said.

Ricardo Pacheco, 63, spent more than two decades on the Baldwin Park City Council before resigning in 2020 as part of his plea deal. Federal prosecutors said he used his elected office to collect cash and funnel other payments through his church and political groups.

The Department of Justice said Pacheco and former Compton City Councilman Isaac Jacob Galvan carried out "corrupt acts while they were elected officials," including accepting and paying bribes for political support and city permits.

Hawaii's Democratic Lieutenant Governor Indicted In State Corruption Investigation

Pacheco was also fined $10,000 and ordered to forfeit $219,755. The FBI seized $83,145 in cash proceeds from him, including $62,900 that Pacheco said he had buried in two places in his backyard, prosecutors said. A restitution hearing is still to be scheduled.

Galvan, 39, received the same 18-month federal prison sentence and was ordered to pay $323,557 in restitution.

Former Gambino Associate Turned New Jersey Councilman Accused Of Running Loansharking Ring While In Office

The case began with the police-union deal.

Between January and October 2018, Pacheco solicited and received $37,900 from a Baldwin Park police officer in exchange for supporting the Baldwin Park Police Association's contract with the city, prosecutors said. The deal was worth at least $4.4 million over three years.

Massachusetts Mayor Charged With Wire Fraud In $1.5M Covid Relief Scheme

The officer was working at the FBI's direction after he and another officer approached the bureau to assist in its corruption investigation, according to the DOJ.

In October 2018, the officer handed Pacheco a $20,000 cash bribe inside an envelope at a Baldwin Park coffee shop, prosecutors said. Pacheco also directed $17,900 in checks to his church and political action committees that were set up in other people's names but controlled by him, according to the DOJ.

Maduro Ally Deported To Us Over Alleged Billion-dollar Corruption Scheme Tied To Oil, Food Program

Pacheco voted for the police association contract in March 2018.

Pacheco later became an FBI informant after agents caught him in a video-recorded sting at the coffee shop, according to the Los Angeles Times.

The outlet reported that Pacheco wore a concealed wire as investigators built cases that led to six indictments involving more than 20 people tied to local government and the marijuana industry.

The outlet also reported that the wider investigation implicated figures including Galvan, a former Baldwin Park city attorney, a Commerce city manager, a San Bernardino County planning commissioner and a marijuana distributor.

The case also uncovered an alleged pay-to-play system around marijuana permits in Baldwin Park.

Former California Mayor Admits To Secretly Working For China, Spreading Beijing Propaganda In Us

The city began allowing marijuana cultivation, manufacturing and distribution in 2017. Prosecutors said Pacheco soon began seeking money from businesses pursuing development agreements and related permits.

Galvan, who was then serving on the Compton City Council, offered consulting services to W&F International Corp., a Diamond Bar import-export business that wanted a marijuana permit in Baldwin Park, prosecutors said.

Galvan then helped facilitate $70,000 in bribes from the company's owner, Yichang Bai, to Pacheco in return for the councilman's votes and political backing, according to the DOJ.

Pacheco delivered, prosecutors said, voting in favor of W&F's permit in June and July 2018 and later supporting the company's effort to relocate its operations.

The payments were obscured through checks from third parties, including checks with blank payee lines, prosecutors said. When Pacheco later sought more money for his legal defense fund, Galvan told Bai the councilman wanted $25,000. Bai agreed to provide $20,000 through seven checks from bank accounts that were not his or W&F's, the DOJ said.

Galvan also admitted he failed to report about $560,525 in income to the IRS from 2017 through 2020. Prosecutors said the scheme caused a tax loss of $115,816.

Bai pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bribery and was sentenced in July to 20 months in federal prison and a $3,000 fine.

title: Barcola - the 'grasshopper' who has overcome setbacks
description: As Liverpool agree a £123m deal for Bradley Barcola, BBC Sport looks at how he has ridden triumphs and setbacks to reach the top with the help of his family.
fullText:
There was a moment, not so long ago, when Bradley Barcola's career appeared to have stalled.

Having earned rave reviews after nailing down a regular starting place in Lyon's starting XI under Peter Bosz, the 20-year-old winger was out of favour and in the reserves by the time the Dutch coach was replaced by Laurent Blanc in October 2022.

According to L'Equipe,, external Barcola was close to joining Swiss club St Gallen in January 2023 in order to get more game time before an act of petulance by a team-mate helped pave his return to the side.

Fans were unhappy with the team's poor form - making first-choice forward Karl Toko Ekambi a target for their frustrations.

The relationship between the Cameroon international and Lyon's ultras fractured further when he stormed down the tunnel and kicked a rubbish bin in frustration after being substituted during a 2-1 home defeat by Strasbourg.

The incident was caught on camera and Toko Ekambi never played for Lyon again.

That presented Barcola with an opportunity which he seized. He started the majority of the remaining matches that season, scoring five times, including a winner at champions-in-waiting Paris St-Germain in April 2023.

Five months after that goal at the Parc des Princes, Barcola was a PSG player.

His reported £38.5m move - two weeks after Brazil forward Neymar swapped Paris for Saudi Arabia - came with Lyon struggling in the table and also unable to sign replacements because of financial restrictions.

"Barcola's first game for PSG was back at Lyon," Pierre-Etienne Minonzio, football journalist for L'Equipe, told BBC Sport.

"He was booed by the Lyon fans because it was just after the transfer. PSG boss Luis Enrique asked Barcola, who was very young at the time, if he was ready to play.

"He said yes, came on as a substitute, and it was impressive."

Barcola, nicknamed the 'grasshopper' because of his speed, agility and slight frame, has since gone on to win three Ligue 1 titles and back-to-back Champions Leagues in his three seasons in the French capital. He broke into the France side two years ago, and scored three times as this summer's World Cup as they reached the semi-finals.

With Liverpool agreeing a £123m deal to sign him, Barcola is on his way to the Premier League.

It has been quite the journey from kicking a ball about as a schoolboy on the playing fields of Vaulx-en-Velin - situated to the east of Lyon - to becoming a superstar worth nine figures. But the path has not been without challenges.

"Barcola is hugely ambitious," added Minonzio.

"He is from a generation of young French talent who are prepared to work hard and want to be a better version of themselves.

"They will do whatever they have to do to get there. They don't ask questions - they just do it."

Why Liverpool are ready to make Barcola third £100m signing

Luis Enrique quiet on Barcola future

Barcola's family have been with him on every step of his journey, from starting out as the shy boy who played for his local team AS Buers Villeurbanne to joining Lyon's academy at the age of eight, to making his Lyon debut 11 years later, to becoming a double Champions League winner with PSG in Budapest in May.

Born Bradley Jean-Manuel Essolisam Addo Barcola on 2 September 2002, he has five siblings - including one other footballer, his older brother Malcolm, 27, a goalkeeper for Ittihad Tanger in Morocco and the Togo national team.

It was their mother who encouraged them to take up football - she would attend their matches and film the brothers playing.

"It's rare but she's the one who gave us passion [for the sport]," Barcola, who looked up to Cristiano Ronaldo and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang, said in an interview with Uefa in 2024.

His father, Yves, had a passion for sport and a strong work ethic, and would gather them in the family living room to watch clips of their matches back together.

Malcolm has spoken about growing up with his younger brother.

"Every weekend, we went to the local stadium," he told newspaper Le Progres., external "My father made Bradley do specific work in front of goal, and me, as a goalkeeper... he made me work too. We complemented each other well."

Long before Barcola, graduates from Lyon's academy included Karim Benzema, who has won multiple Champions Leagues with Real Madrid and the Ballon d'Or, Arsenal FA Cup winner Alexandre Lacazette, and France 2018 World Cup winners Samuel Umtiti and Corentin Tolisso.

More recent graduates include Manchester City forward Rayan Cherki and Chelsea full-back Malo Gusto.

Aged 17, Barcola scored 11 goals in 17 league matches for Lyon's Under-19 team before signing his first professional contract two years later in 2021.

It was a huge moment for the Barcola family.

During his rise to fame and fortune, Barcola has spoken about the importance of his family in keeping him grounded.

When the player was roundly criticised for missing chances against Newcastle in the Champions League in his first season at PSG, he turned to his family for support.

"My parents and I talk about everything," Barcola said in an interview with French newspaper Le Parisien. "As soon as something goes wrong, on or off the pitch, we talk about it. I've got my older brother, too.

"When things aren't going so well, I need to see them and get their advice.

"When they tell me 'you're messing up', it's because they're right. And when they tell me I've played well, it's because I have. I don't listen to what's said outside."

Asked about his son's reaction to the criticism following the Newcastle match, Yves Barcola said: "We talked to him about it, it's the kind of thing that doesn't affect him. That's what he tells us, it pushes him to do more.

"He's never been given anything in his young career, he's always had to earn things with his patience and qualities."

Paris St-Germain boss Luis Enrique has described Barcola as a "balanced person, very sensible, humble, hard-working, with great family values".

"After Newcastle at the Parc, he was very criticised, unfairly, and that did not reflect reality," added Luis Enrique. "He was able to calmly manage the difficult moments post-Newcastle in the best possible way."

What strengths might Barcola bring to Anfield?

'Liverpool have to get Barcola deal done'

Barcola is the statement signing Liverpool fans have craved all summer.

With his expensive price tag, however, comes pressure.

He will be expected to hit the ground running, but he does have form against Premier League opposition.

Barcola has come up against numerous English clubs during his time at PSG. He scored in a 4-2 Champions League win over Manchester City in January 2025 before finding the net in each leg against Chelsea in the last-16 last season.

Liverpool and their new boss Andoni Iraola will take positives that Barcola settled so quickly after his high-profile move to PSG.

"He went to Paris St-Germain for something like 50m euros, which was a huge amount considering he had only played something like one full season in Ligue 1," said Minonzio.

"It was an insane amount of money for someone who had not really done anything, but Luis Enrique saw something in him.

"Luis Enrique said: 'Whatever it costs, we need him because he has huge potential.'

"Full credit to Luis Enrique because he saw things a lot of people didn't see.

"Barcola started well at PSG but after some months he had some issues because opposition defenders noticed that he was always doing the same kind of dribble.

"He was aware of that and he managed to change and have a wider range of tricks.

"He has a lot more qualities than two or three years ago."

Minonzio added: "Personally I think Liverpool is a good fit for Barcola, especially because of Iraola. He is so good at improving players and Barcola is not the finished product.

"Sometimes he runs and runs and runs, and then his finishing is not always good. He has to improve and I think he will.

"It was exactly the same with Ousmane Dembele. Two or three years ago, Dembele was so good at dribbling and running, but sometimes when he was in front of goal he was making bad choices.

"Barcola is a bit like that in the finishing aspect of his game, but he will improve with the right manager - and I think Iraola is the right manager."

Sylvain Ripoll was Barcola's France Under-21 coach in 2023.

"He's very endearing, always in a good mood," he said of Liverpool's new signing.

"He might seem a little reserved, but he has character on the pitch and in his decision-making. He brings something different to the table, all with an exceptional mindset."

Luis Enrique has gone on record as saying signing Barcola in 2023 was a "gamble".

title: 'Unbelievable' - Stephenson & Bellew react to Hrgovic's stoppage of Itauma
description: Shakur Stevenson and Tony Bellew believe Moses Itauma still has what it takes to become a world champion after losing to Filip Hrgovic for the IBF heavyweight title.
fullText:
Shakur Stevenson and Tony Bellew believe Moses Itauma showed enough in defeat by Filip Hrgovic to suggest he will become a heavyweight world champion.

Itauma made a fast start at London's O2 Arena and controlled large parts of the contest for the vacant IBF title, but eventually ran out of steam and was stopped by Hrgovic in round nine.

The Briton's speed and power caught the eye early in the bout but once he broke new ground - going beyond the sixth round for the first time in his career - the wheels began to come off.

Hrgovic was outpunched in every round until the decisive ninth when he seized his moment to become Croatia's first heavyweight world champion.

BBC Radio 5 Live's coverage of the night ended with Richie Woodhall, Ronald McIntosh and Steve Bunce offering up one word each to describe the night.

"Incredible," former super-middleweight world champion Woodhall said.

"Unbelievable," added commentator McIntosh, while Bunce signed off with "unforgettable".

Relive Hrgovic's dramatic stoppage win over Itauma to claim IBF heavyweight title

Itauma punches himself out against Hrgovic in world-title fight

Many expected Itauma, who stepped into the ring with a perfect record of 14 wins as a professional, to be coronated as the next British heavyweight star - although Hrgovic was rightly touted as his biggest test to date.

Aged 21, Itauma was seeking to become the second-youngest heavyweight world champion of all-time and Britain's second-youngest world champion.

But lack of experience against a seasoned Hrgovic proved Itauma's undoing.

Hype around Itauma has been building since winning his pro debut in just 23 seconds in January 2023.

A string of highlight knockouts - winning 12 of his previous 14 bouts inside six rounds - had propelled the Chatham fighter to world-title level in quick fashion.

Despite coming up short against 34-year-old Hrgovic, he is still being tipped to reach the pinnacle of boxing's glamour division.

"Unbelievable talent and skills," four-weight world champion Stevenson wrote on X.

"He's young and will be a champion one day if he learns from that. He throws every punch at 100mph and that can be a gift and a curse, Especially in the heavyweights division!"

Fellow Briton Tony Bellew, who was a cruiserweight world champion but ended his career at heavyweight, was also keen to focus on the positives.

"Moses Itauma will be world champion! He will learn so much from tonight," Bellew posted on X.

"The biggest thing I'll take from tonight is just how brave and tough Moses was, we knew Filip was super tough. Tonight we learned Moses is also tough, once he learns to pace a 12-round bout, he's gonna rule for a while! Filip Hrgovic's chin needs to studied."

Itauma told BBC Sport in the weeks before his heavyweight title fight that he had never even sparred 12 rounds, and it showed as he grew fatigued with each round that passed.

Trainer Ben Davison almost threw in the towel early in the ninth round as Itauma staggered around the ring, but he had second thoughts.

It was only moments later that the towel did come in as referee Howard Foster had stepped in to wave off the contest with Itauma unable to stand without the ropes to aid him.

Chris Eubank Jr wrote on X: "Not sure what happened tonight. Moses was fighting well and then gassed out it seems… at his young age this should simply not be happening. Time to rethink his training camp moving forward I think."

title: Boreham Wood accept Vardy-beating record fee for Abdulmalik
description: Swedish club Djurgardens agree a National League record fee thought to be in excess of £1.5m to sign winger Abdul Abdulmalik from Boreham Wood.
fullText:
Swedish club Djurgardens have agreed a National League record fee thought to be in excess of £1.5m to sign winger Abdul Abdulmalik from Boreham Wood.

The 23-year-old's move breaks the record fee paid for a fifth-tier player in England, set in 2012 when Leicester City paid Fleetwood Town £1m for Jamie Vardy.

Abdulmalik is currently in Sweden completing a medical after the deal was agreed on Sunday morning.

The forward enjoyed a breakthrough season in 2025-26, scoring 17 goals and providing 10 assists as Boreham Wood reached the National League play-off final, where he scored and set up a goal at Wembley.

The agreement also brings to an end a long-running transfer saga, with the Hertfordshire club having rejected bids of £1m and £1.5m for the former Millwall academy player earlier this summer.

Abdulmalik said: "I'm ready for the next challenge. I'm ready to prove to myself and those around me that I'm capable of reaching the top."

He scored in his final appearance for Boreham Wood in mid-August but subsequently made himself unavailable for selection in an attempt to secure a move.

Clubs in England, including Peterborough United, had also expressed an interest.

Abdulmalik was previously an England Under-17s international but was released by Millwall in 2024 and had an unsuccessful trial at Portsmouth.

Stockholm-based Djurgardens are currently fifth in the Allsvenskan - which runs from April to November - but have two games in hand on the majority of their rivals and remain in contention to qualify for Europe.

title: How Sabalenka could lose No 1 ranking at US Open
description: Will Aryna Sabalenka rediscover her mojo? How will Carlos Alcaraz's comeback go? And can Novak Djokovic win? It's time for the 2026 US Open singles.
fullText:
All was bright in Aryna Sabalenka's world when she completed a rare 'Sunshine Double' earlier this season.

Becoming only the fifth woman to win the Indian Wells and Miami titles back-to-back, Sabalenka emphasised her position as the dominant player on the WTA Tour and created a 3,000-point lead at the top of the world rankings.

But a difficult period quickly followed - seemingly out of nowhere - leaving the 28-year-old Belarusian clinging on to her position going into the US Open, which starts on Sunday.

Two-time defending champion Sabalenka returns to New York with a 17-7 win-loss record since the Miami triumph, including a chastening French Open quarter-final exit and a disheartening defeat in the Wimbledon fourth round.

It is a record far below the four-time major winner's lofty standards.

With 2,000 points to defend at Flushing Meadows and Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina now trailing by only 434, Sabalenka must win again to extend her 99-week run as the world number one.

Asked if she felt confident she can rediscover her mojo on the hard courts on which she has thrived, Sabalenka said: "Absolutely. These tough lessons are definitely going to make me way, way stronger and working even harder."

Tough US Open draw for Alcaraz - who else plays who?

'A generational icon' - why wildcards abound for Venus Williams

How to follow US Open on the BBC

Sabalenka's four Grand Slam singles titles - two Australian Open and two US Open triumphs, all on hard courts - are more than most players can dream of.

However, she has also lost four major finals and six semi-finals, despite a consistency on the biggest stages that is unrivalled among her peers.

The concern in recent months has been Sabalenka's mental focus disappearing in less pressurised situations.

This was most recently apparent in her Cincinnati Open fourth-round defeat by 20-year-old Czech opponent Sara Bejlek. Sabalenka led 5-1 in a first-set tie-break and 4-1 in the second set, but continued to lack composure in the rallies as Bejlek rallied to win 7-6 (9-7) 6-4.

At her previous tournament in Toronto, she lost to Russian world number 19 Ekaterina Alexandrova in the last 16 as her serve crumbled.

During the clay-court swing, Sabalenka capitulated after winning the first set against Hailey Baptiste in Madrid, Sorana Cirstea in Rome and, most notably, Diana Shnaider at Roland Garros.

"I work on my mental side of the game. I've been trying to reset my mind and to come back stronger," a bullish Sabalenka said in New York.

"It's only a matter of time for me to come back."

The drop-off in Sabalenka's results have opened the door for Rybakina, who beat the Belarusian to win the Australian Open in January, to take over as world number one.

Rybakina might not even have to win a match at Flushing Meadows to do that, as she has fewer ranking points to defend than Sabalenka.

However, there are questions over her fitness because of an ankle injury sustained in the Cincinnati quarter-finals.

Rybakina can secure the number one ranking if her nearest rivals - Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff - do not win the title.

If Sabalenka does retain the title, Rybakina would still also rise to the top by reaching the semi-finals.

Pegula, 32, has been ultra-consistent for several seasons without landing a major title, but the 2024 finalist hopes her runs to the Washington and Cincinnati finals will provide the platform for another crack at her home Slam.

Gauff, who beat Pegula to the Cincinnati trophy last week, already has the experience of winning in New York after claiming her first major there in 2023.

Twelve months ago, the 22-year-old American's game was clouded by uncertainty but returns with more confidence and fluidity in her serve.

Beneath the leading quartet, the rest of the top 10 also hold either a Grand Slam or WTA 1,000 title - a group led by French Open winner Mirra Andreeva, Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova and six-time major winner Iga Swiatek.

"You can just see how the depth is pretty crazy," said Pegula.

Williams sisters given US Open doubles wildcard

Newlywed Boulter won't repeat Murray's ring mistake

For the third Grand Slam in a row, the rivalry between Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz has been put on hold.

The pair swept all eight major titles between them in 2024 and 2025, with Alcaraz extending that run with victory at this year's Australian Open.

But the pair have not competed at the same Grand Slam since.

Alcaraz missed the French Open and Wimbledon with a wrist injury, and makes his comeback from a four-month absence in New York.

A day after the 23-year-old Spaniard announced his plan to return, Sinner revealed he had been ruled out with a knee issue.

"It's kind of weird. We are not going see each other for, like, six months now, seven months," said Alcaraz.

Sinner's absence and the uncertainty around Alcaraz's fitness will galvanise the rest of the chasing pack - particularly 39-year-old Novak Djokovic.

The Serb great, a 24-time Grand Slam champion, insists he has not put an "expiry date" on his extraordinary career. He continues to put himself in the mix for titles as he looks to finally land a standalone record 25th victory which would move him clear of Australia's Margaret Court on the all-time list.

He has reached at least the semi-finals in six of the past seven Slams, but has not gone all the way since triumphing at the 2023 US Open.

Germany's Alexander Zverev leads the seedings as he looks to reach a third straight major final, having won his first Slam at the French Open before losing to Sinner at Wimbledon.

Canadian Open champion Ben Shelton and Cincinnati finalist Frances Tiafoe lead a strong American challenge, while 2024 finalist Taylor Fritz is another hope capable of ending a 23-year wait for a home men's champion.

title: Martinez is eighth Chelsea-Villa deal in four years
description: After Emiliano Martinez's move, BBC Sport looks at why Aston Villa and Chelsea have become one of the Premier League’s busiest transfer partnerships since 2022.
fullText:
Chelsea have signed Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa for £7.5m - the eighth deal between the two clubs in the past four years.

The 33-year-old, who won the World Cup in 2022, has moved to Stamford Bridge on a three-year deal.

Former Arsenal goalkeeper Martinez joined Villa in 2020 and made 256 appearances, helping the club win the Europa League last season.

"I'm delighted to be at this football club," Martinez said.

"Coming to Chelsea, for me and my family, was an easy decision to make and I'm just over the moon - I can't wait to get started.

'I want to be successful here. I'm someone who wants to win at everything I do and I want to bring that here to this football club because it's a football club that wins titles, so I think it's a good match."

Martinez's move to Chelsea comes after Nicolas Jackson's transfer the other way last week.

No two Premier League clubs have exchanged more players, on permanent or loan deals, in the past four years.

The relationship began after Chelsea's owners, BlueCo, took control of the club in 2022 and signed Carney Chukwuemeka from Villa for £20m that summer. Ian Maatsen (£37.5m, to Villa), Omari Kellyman (£19m, to Chelsea) and Axel Disasi (a £5m loan deal, to Villa) subsequently moved between the clubs.

This summer alone has brought four more deals. Morgan Rogers completed a £117m move Chelsea, while Alejandro Garnacho joined Villa on loan with a conditional obligation to buy in a deal worth around £43m.

Jackson then moved to Villa for £65m, before Martinez followed.

Since 2022, Chelsea have paid Aston Villa £163.5m for players. Villa have spent £102.5m on Chelsea players including Axel Disasi's loan fee. That figure could rise to £150.5m should certain criteria be met to make Garnacho's loan move permanent. Chelsea believe the terms are easily reachable.

Chelsea and Villa have done business before. Tammy Abraham, Ross Barkley, Danny Drinkwater, Ryan Bertrand, Steve Sidwell and Andy Townsend are among those to have moved between the clubs during the Premier League era, while John Terry joined Villa after leaving Chelsea.

But the recent volume of business between the clubs has not gone unnoticed elsewhere in the Premier League, at a time when both have had to navigate domestic and European financial regulations. One source told BBC Sport that a number of club executives have raised questions about the frequency of the dealings.

There is no suggestion, though, that either club have broken any rules.

BBC Sport has approached Chelsea and Aston Villa for comment.

BBC Sport has counted every permanent transfer and loan between Premier League clubs since the summer of 2022, restricting the analysis to the 15 sides who have been in the top flight throughout that period.

There is a tie at the top: Chelsea have done eight deals with Villa, and another eight with Brighton.

Newcastle United and Nottingham Forest are next on six, followed by Arsenal and Chelsea on five.

Chelsea feature in six of the 10 busiest club pairings, illustrating the scale of their player trading since the BlueCo consortium completed its takeover.

BlueCo's £4.25bn purchase of Chelsea ended Roman Abramovich's 19-year ownership and ushered in a period of significant squad turnover.

But Villa's close relationship with Chelsea also has a more specific explanation.

Chelsea co-owner Behdad Eghbali and Villa owner Nassef Sawiris have developed a close working relationship and have communicated directly over transfer business.

That relationship has spanned several transfer windows and included Rogers' move to Stamford Bridge this summer.

Chelsea did not have a clear run at Rogers, though - as Arsenal also wanted to sign him, and it was the player's decision to move to Stamford Bridge.

Uefa has the power to scrutinise transfers completed between the same clubs within a 45-day period. Garnacho's move to Villa - on an initial loan deal - came two days after Rogers signed for Chelsea. Jackson's permanent transfer went through 38 days after the Rogers one.

But a timeline on its own is not evidence that the deals were in any way related.

Villa, for instance, could point to their long-held interest in Jackson, who previously worked with head coach Unai Emery at Villarreal.

Chelsea, meanwhile, could argue their interest in Martinez was independent of previous dealings with Villa and would have been pursued regardless of the club he played for. The goalkeeper had attracted interest from Juventus earlier in the window, with a finger injury understood to have scuppered a move.

There are broader reasons why domestic transfers remain attractive, but money is often the biggest factor.

Premier League clubs generally have greater spending power than most teams elsewhere in Europe, meaning another English side may be among the few buyers capable of meeting the fee and wage demands of a selling club.

That can make domestic deals particularly attractive when clubs are trying to move on high-value players. Signing from within the league also reduces some of the uncertainty, with recruitment teams already familiar with a player's qualities and performances.

Yet even in a league where domestic trading is commonplace, the frequency of deals between Villa and Chelsea stands out.

title: Heavyweight Itauma handed harsh world-title lesson
description: British heavyweight Moses Itauma was taught a harsh lesson at world level - what can he learn from defeat and where does the 21-year-old go next?
fullText:
Moses Itauma was still a schoolboy when he would turn up at boxing gyms in his uniform and give seasoned professionals a hiding.

On Saturday night at the O2 Arena, the 21-year-old was finally given an education, as the Briton ran out of gas and the granite experience of Filip Hrgovic carried the Croatian to the vacant IBF heavyweight title.

The referee waved off the fight as Itauma's corner threw in the towel in the ninth round. But for long spells, Itauma was the quicker, sharper and more assured fighter, repeatedly finding Hrgovic with the left hand and showing exactly why so many inside boxing believe he has the tools to reach the very top.

Yet what made the contest so compelling was the growing sense that, even while Itauma was winning rounds, he was drifting closer to defeat.

'Unbelievable' - Stephenson, Bellew & others react to Hrgovic's stoppage of Itauma

Wardley-Dubois rematch set for 17 October in London

His mouth opened in search of air and the spring disappeared from his legs. Hrgovic, hardened by the kind of difficult nights Itauma had never experienced, simply stayed there and waited for the younger man's body to betray him.

The sight afterwards was a sobering one as Itauma - who suffered a first defeat in his 15th pro fight - left the arena on a stretcher, before being taken to hospital.

"It's precautionary that he's gone to the hospital. That's what we always do to make sure because the most important thing is the boxer's health," promoter Frank Warren said.

"He's done something to his leg as well and he was quite tired. It was a high paced, fast fight for both the guys."

The remarkable night should not be remembered as the moment Itauma was exposed as incapable of operating at world level - his boxing showed the opposite.

What it exposed was the difference between possessing world-level talent and having the conditioning, experience and ring craft required to manage a 12-round world-title fight.

It would be too simplistic - and unfair - to say Hrgovic won the fight purely through mind games, but the 34-year-old had succeeded in making the build-up uncomfortable.

Hrgovic spent fight week repeatedly attacking Itauma's age, dismissing him as "just a kid". As the week wore on, Itauma looked increasingly irritated and eventually lost his composure at the weigh-in, shoving Hrgovic before the Croatian responded with a slap.

Itauma prides himself on being unusually cerebral for a heavyweight. He reads psychology and self-help books, talks openly about sharpening his mind and appears to spend far more time analysing himself than most 21-year-olds.

But there is always a danger that deep thinking becomes overthinking, something Anthony Joshua has been accused of repeatedly during the latter stages of his career.

Whether the pre-fight barbs played any part or not, Itauma's gameplan once the bell rang was clear; he wanted to end the night early.

"Someone said to me he doesn't feel like he'd win a world title unless he knocks him out. I didn't like that," Warren said.

That mindset was understandable because it had served Itauma extraordinarily well until now. But perhaps Hrgovic had been underestimated by almost everybody - Itauma, the media, pundits, former fighters and bookmakers who installed the Briton as a heavy favourite.

Hrgovic is an Olympic bronze medallist who went 12 hard rounds with the giant Zhilei Zhang, while against Daniel Dubois - the only defeat on his record - he was leading on two of the three scorecards before the fight was stopped because of cuts.

'El Animal' knew what it felt like to be hurt, to become tired and to remain in a fight when things were going badly. Itauma did not.

The eighth round summed up both Itauma's extraordinary talent and his lack of experience. He threw more punches than in any other round of the fight, pouring what remained of his energy into trying to remove a man who had already demonstrated that he was exceptionally difficult to remove.

"He was throwing too much. He was fighting like an amateur," Hrgovic said afterwards. "I knew I needed to endure it. I need to stay there. He will get tired and I'll get him in the later rounds."

There are questions about the Chatham fighter's preparation, too. Itauma - who had never gone beyond six rounds professionally - admitted before the fight that he had never even sparred 12 rounds.

His conditioning was clearly not where it needed to be for a championship fight and responsibility for that cannot rest solely with the fighter - it also falls on the experienced team entrusted with preparing him.

Itauma showed that many of the qualities which looked spectacular against lesser opposition still worked against a genuine world-level heavyweight.

He proved he can take a punch - there was no single blow that suddenly revealed a fragile chin. His hand speed troubled Hrgovic and he made the Zagreb fighter look slow.

So with those positives in mind, where does he go from here?

"Don't give up. Don't lose confidence. Get a few easy fights, easy wins. Build again and learn off these mistakes. You can't box like an amateur. It's a 12-round fight, you need to pace yourself," was Hrgovic's advice.

Warren remains convinced that Itauma is one of the most exceptional talents he has encountered, pointing towards two-time world champion Dubois as a prime example of a heavyweight who rebuilt successfully after painful setbacks.

But British boxing has seen the other side of that story too, of course - where fighters like David Price were once regarded as the country's next great heavyweight hope before successive defeats damaged an aura they never fully recovered.

Audiences will now scrutinise Itauma's every move, his breathing and how he paces a fight. That vulnerability may actually make him a more compelling fighter to follow.

The aura of untouchable perfection is gone. The schoolboy has been taught a lesson and now we will find out what he learns from it.

title: Tottenham make Ndiaye move with Richarlison set for Everton
description: Tottenham are in advanced talks to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton, with Richarlison set to move in the opposite direction as part of separate negotiations.
fullText:
Tottenham are in advanced talks to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton, with Richarlison set to move in the opposite direction as part of separate negotiations.

Although a deal for Nidaye is largely agreed between the two clubs, it remains unclear whether he will make the switch to north London, with Manchester City among the clubs to have expressed an interest.

City have also held talks to sign Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, another Spurs target, although the Reds would need to secure a replacement before sanctioning any move.

Everton are open to selling Ndiaye, 26, after he rejected multiple contract offers and held talks with Saudi club Al-Hilal earlier this summer.

Meanwhile, Everton have agreed terms in principle to re-sign Brazilian striker Richarlison after he told Spurs head coach Roberto de Zerbi "too many times that he wants to leave".

The Brazil international has entered the final year of his Tottenham contract and would provide competition for first-choice striker Thierno Barry, with uncertainty surrounding Beto's future at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

Everton are also growing increasingly confident of completing a loan deal to bring Jack Grealish back from Manchester City, although the precise terms of any agreement remain complicated as the England international enters the final year of his contract at Etihad Stadium.

Grealish has prioritised a return to Everton, where he spent last season on loan, over the option of rejoining his boyhood club Aston Villa, who have also expressed an interest.

The club are also targeting a right-back, with talks over a move for Fulham's Kenny Tete reopened after he came close to joining last summer.

Fulham are already assessing potential replacements and have entered talks to sign Andrei Ratiu.

It is part of a chain of interconnected Premier League deals before Tuesday's transfer deadline.

Richarlison is one of three players who De Zerbi says have asked to leave Tottenham.

He, Kevin Danso and Pape Matar Sarr have all been linked with moves away from Spurs and none were included in De Zerbi's matchday squad as Tottenham lost 2-0 at home to Newcastle on Saturday.

Asked about their status after the loss, De Zerbi said: "Richarlison, I don't know. He said too many times he wants to leave.

"Danso came to me two days ago and he said wants to leave and Pape Sarr the same, but he suffered a small injury, but he is almost ready to train.

"I have very good relationships but if they want to leave, they have to bring the solution, the economic solution, to the club, and they can go."

Spurs have spent more than £300m this summer in an effort to restore their competitive edge following back-to-back 17th-place Premier League finishes.

But Tottenham are bottom of the table, having lost their first two games to Brentford and Newcastle and failing to score a goal.

With 11 goals, Richarlison was Tottenham's top scorer last season, and a key figure during their struggle for Premier League survival, which was secured on the final day.

Earlier in August, De Zerbi said that the Brazilian was uncertain about his future, noting that, "it's not easy to find another striker like Richarlison".

Last week, Manchester City striker Omar Marmoush joined Spurs on loan and he replaced Richarlison in De Zerbi's starting XI against Newcastle.

Danso's first-team opportunities may be limited this season as Marcos Senesi and Jan Paul van Hecke arrive to challenge for his place in central defence, where Micky van de Ven's spot was secured by the signing of a new contract and the award of the captaincy.

Sunderland made an offer to take Danso, who has 36 Austria caps, on a season-long loan - but Spurs rejected it.

In midfield, Sarr's chance to play has been impacted by the arrivals of Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali early in the window, as Tottenham kicked off their a statement summer of transfers by breaking their club record fee twice in one week.

The Senegal international, 23, has attracted interest from a number of clubs, including several in the Premier League and Turkish side Besiktas.

However, Juventus are understood to be confident of winning the race for his signature on a loan deal that includes a conditional obligation to buy.

Everton call off Armstrong sale after fan backlash

title: Everton call off Armstrong sale after fan backlash
description: Everton have called off a proposed deal to sell midfielder Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest following a backlash from the club's supporters.
fullText:
Everton have called off a proposed deal to sell midfielder Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest following a backlash from the club's supporters.

Forest made a bid of £40m plus a potential sell-on clause for the England Under-19 international, who is regarded as one of the brightest prospects to emerge from Finch Farm in recent years.

The news enraged Everton supporters, who sang Armstrong's name throughout Saturday's draw at Bournemouth and said there would be a "riot" if he was sold.

Everton's board, led by chair Dan Friedkin, eventually decided to reject Forest's bid – with the owner at the forefront of the discussions.

'Supporters aren't always wrong' - Moyes on Everton fans' anger

Are Moyes and Everton's owners on same page?

Armstrong has made 24 appearances for Everton and played 87 minutes against the Cherries before he was replaced by Charly Alcaraz.

Speaking after the game Toffees boss David Moyes said he understood the fans' frustration and appeared to suggest the decision was out of his hands.

"I think you always have to consider supporters; supporters aren't always wrong," Moyes.

"But then there are also times where I've had people at clubs who are really powerful and make difficult decisions.

"Managers have to make decisions on players sometimes and they feel like huge decisions. But there are sometimes bigger decisions to be made and the club will, I'm sure, make what they think is the right one.

"If I'd say something to them (the fans), I'd say their manager's an Evertonian."

Moyes has been frustrated by the club's lack of signings and he made it clear he wanted reinforcements after the Carabao Cup second-round win against Preston on Wednesday.

The Toffees have signed Hayden Hackney from Middlesbrough for an initial £16m and fellow midfielder Christian Norgaard from Arsenal for £7m

Tyrique George and Merlin Rohl signed permanent deals after loan spells last season, while Brennan Johnson joined from Crystal Palace in a swap deal with Dwight McNeil.

Talks are ongoing and moving forward between Everton and Manchester City for Jack Grealish to return before the deadline, with another loan the most likely option at this stage.

However, the club have yet to sign a right-back to replace Seamus Coleman, though they have revived interest in Kenny Tete, who turned down the Toffees to sign a new deal at Fulham last year.

Everton's decision to reject Nottingham Forest's offer for teenager Harrison Armstrong has headed off the possibility of open revolt against owners The Friedkin Group from a furious fanbase.

The revelation that Everton had received a £40m bid from Forest for the gifted 19-year-old, and it was under consideration, sparked an instant backlash from fans angry at the idea the club's best homegrown product for years could be sold.

Instead, after a day of drama on and off the field, Everton's board - led by chairman and billionaire owner Dan Friedkin - decided to unanimously reject Forest's approach and keep Armstrong.

Everton's fans made their feelings clear during the 1-1 draw at Bournemouth. The reaction was so loud, and toxic, that it is sure to have been heard by Everton's delegation at The Vitality Stadium and relayed back to the hierarchy in the United States.

It is highly unlikely to be coincidence that a deal that looked to be advancing was then stopped in its tracks.

And it will also pacify manager David Moyes, whose mood looked ominous post-match at Bournemouth, as he will now keep a young talent regarded as a key part of the club's future.

Everton's supporters may reluctantly accept that important players could be prised away by Champions League clubs, but the notion of Nottingham Forest being able to do the same added another layer to their fury.

Forest are one of the club's Everton and their fans would hope to surpass, not bolster them by selling one of their crown jewels to them.

For The Friedkin Group, it is a PR catastrophe avoided.
